editorials.title: New fault lines: On Manipur’s Kuki-Zo–Naga conflict
editorials.passage:
In the three years since the conflagration of May 2023 hardened into a fault line between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities, Manipur has traversed a slow path towards peace between them. After nearly a year of President’s Rule gave way in February 2026 to a Bharatiya Janata Party-led government under a new Chief Minister, Yumnam Khemchand Singh , attempts to engineer a thaw gathered pace with the everyday violence between the communities abating. Yet, many of those displaced in 2023 remain in relief camps; an RTI reply puts those dead in these camps at over 700, many due to the lack of access to basic health care and adequate nutrition. Even so, there have been tentative and encouraging openings towards rebuilding normalcy. On September 2, two Kuki-Zo MLAs attended the Assembly session — the first time since legislators from the community began boycotting it following the attacks in Imphal at the start of the ethnic conflict. In doing so they defied a directive from the Kuki-Zo civil society organisation, the Kuki Inpi Manipur, to continue the boycott until there was a concession on the demand for a separate administration. The two MLAs seem to acknowledge that it is time to reopen the political space even if differences persist, and for this, their presence in the Assembly must be welcomed.

Yet, these moves have coincided with a new ethnic fault line in Manipur. Since February, violence between the Naga and Kuki-Zo communities — which began as localised disputes — has spread across the hill districts. Till July, at least 15 Kuki-Zo people, 11 Nagas, three security personnel and a truck driver were killed; more have died in the last two months. Houses in Naga and Kuki-Zo villages have been burnt down and the newly displaced have moved into camps. Blockades imposed by partisans of the communities against the other have held up essentials and medicines, with the smaller Kuki-Zo community the worse affected. Health centres in the hills have been left dysfunctional. This echoes the Naga-Kuki violence of the 1990s, now revived by armed groups claiming to act on behalf of their respective communities and resurrecting arguments over who controls the hills and whose customary laws prevail there. With its tenure ending soon and Assembly elections due next year, the State government must move quickly to contain this outbreak of hostilities. It must work with civil society to lower the rhetoric — reportage from the ground suggests a weariness with the violence across communities – while acting against the armed groups with the help of the security forces. Those imposing blockades must be deterred by the force of law. Criminal law must apply equally across communities in the hills, and the safety and welfare of civilians must be guaranteed irrespective of ethnicity.

editorials.title: Complex priorities: On UPI transactions, MDR charges
editorials.passage:
The Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) charges announced for UPI transactions show how political considerations can dilute economic benefits. In a quest to preempt political attacks, the rate structure announced by the National Payments Corporation of India has been made overly complex. From October 15, the new rates will apply only to UPI payments of ₹2,000 or more made at merchants. As such, the charge is limited to only about 2.5% of all UPI transactions, which is a welcome limitation. Yet, within this, the rules have created different gradations. UPI payments made at small merchants earning less than ₹1 lakh a month are exempt. Those made to merchants operating in certain essential sectors will attract a flat MDR charge instead of the 0.4% applicable on other sectors. Capital market payments above ₹2,000 will attract a different MDR. These are clearly designed keeping political backlash in mind. However, they raise some important doubts among merchants, and could potentially slow the adoption of UPI in India. For example, the rules are not clear on what happens to a small merchant who crosses the ₹1 lakh a month turnover threshold, which is a low limit at today’s prices. Who is monitoring their incomes? This will either increase the compliance burden on small merchants, or involve a new mechanism for real-time transaction-checking that banks will have to develop. In the short run, it will likely result in small merchants simply refusing to accept UPI until greater clarity emerges.

The government has also instructed banks to make sure that merchants do not pass on this charge to customers. But it has not specified how banks are expected to check whether merchants tweak their prices to absorb this additional charge. A back-of-the-envelope calculation based on past trends suggests that the MDR will yield an upper limit of ₹2,400 crore of monthly revenue for the payments ecosystem. The sector-wise flat rates and reduced rates will likely result in a lower amount. The government has denied any U.S. pressure to bring these rates to favour American credit card companies. Yet, the data suggest that the benefit will largely accrue to private banks and U.S.-owned UPI apps. There is still an argument to be made for the Reserve Bank of India to foot this bill from the vast surpluses it generates every year. Maintaining vital payment infrastructure is surely a good use of these funds. However, if the government persists in implementing this charge, it should certainly simplify the structure. There is still time before its rollout. The Goods and Services Tax experience shows that rate complexity hits small businesses the hardest.

editorials.title: Infighting following Tata Sons meet bodes ill for Group, economy
editorials.passage: The cloud of uncertainty hanging over India’s biggest business conglomerate just got darker as more of the infighting within the Tata Group tumbled out in the open. Even as the Tata Sons board on Thursday decided to reappoint N Chandrasekaran to the chair for a fresh five-year term—raising hopes of a resolution to the leadership issue—Tata Trusts led by Noel Tata termed the appointment illegal according to the company’s Articles of Association. Earlier on Thursday, the board also went against Noel’s wishes while giving the go-ahead for Tata Sons’ stock listing. Four of the six board members voted in favour of both proposals. Noel voted against, while another Tata Trusts nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted in favour.There is, however, another twist in this long-running chamber drama. Tata Sons’ Articles of Association mandate that no decision can be taken by the board without the backing of all nominees from Sir Dorabji Tata Trusts and Sir Ratan Tata Trusts. Also, these decisions will have to be ratified by the annual shareholders’ meeting of Tata Sons, where the trusts can call the shots.For themselves, the trusts made no bones about their unhappiness over the day’s events. They stated that the board could not lawfully hold a meeting or pass a resolution on the chairman’s appointment or reappointment unless both their nominee directors voted in favour..The group now stares at a longer period of ambiguity as regulatory pressure to go public grows. The Tata Trusts vehemently oppose the listing of Tata Sons, which would bring on greater scrutiny from shareholders and regulators. A listing also means the trusts would have to loosen their grip over the $230-billion business empire. With the RBI rejecting the trusts’ last-ditch attempt to avoid Tata Sons’ listing, the only option for the group is a legal battle with the regulator. The RBI has already filed a caveat in the Bombay High Court anticipating that the Tatas may move court against its directive.The country can ill afford to see the Tata Group marred by infighting. It’s not only bad optics for the company, but the situation is harmful for the broader economy in which the Tatas are at the forefront of India’s strategic sectors such as semiconductors, defence, software and electronics. It may be time for an arbitrator—not a court—to find an amicable solution..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: DKS unveils vision for 2037, has to deliver by 2028 poll
editorials.passage: It has been rollercoaster for Karnataka Chief Minister D K Shivakumar during his first 100 days in the hot seat. The milestone has been marked by new schemes, public measures and not a few controversies. Over the past three months, Shivakumar has announced major decisions, cleared investments of over ₹43,000 crore and unveiled a vision for building a $1-trillion state economy with what he terms ‘druda sankalpa’ (literally, strong resolve). Knowing well that he cannot rest on the goodwill of the five welfare guarantees that are synonymous with former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah, Shivakumar introduced a sixth Bhu Guarantee scheme to digitise and regularise land records. Upgrade of irregular property records to compliant status brought in some much-needed revenues. The initial dynamism has not worn out yet—the administration is still cracking the whip on garbage and debris littering, clearing footpaths and fixing potholes, with Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda at the helm. But some of Shivakumar’s big-ticket projects for Bengaluru have run into opposition. The 7,500-acre Bidadi township project has been put on the back-burner and the Parks Amendment Bill has been withdrawn. The opposition also forced U-turn on a tunnel road scything through the city’s prime lung-space of Lalbagh. These retractions have somewhat soured the image of a hands-on Chief Minister. .The political interregnum has been tense, too, with DKS inducting former minister B Nagendra, who is facing charges related to a financial fraud at Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation. A sustained opposition campaign forced Nagendra to resign for a second time. There is also fresh trouble in the form of Enforcement Directorate raids on Public Works Minister Satish Jarkiholi, whose business interests abroad are being probed. Housing Minister Zameer Ahmed Khan is being questioned on the I-Monetary Advisory ponzi scheme that ended former Congressman Roshan Baig’s career. On personnel choices, another sticking point is the lack of women in the ministry. DKS’s vision for the state by 2037—featuring Maha Sankalpa and Nava Sankalpa for the economy and the Mekedatu and Yettinahole irrigation projects—is being likened to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Viksit Bharat 2047. But with just over a year left to prove his mettle before the next Assembly election, Shivakumar is prioritising high-visibility development projects. The people of the state are waiting for the results..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | A bent shape of you
editorials.passage: When Ed Sheeran gave in to pro-Israel billionaire Robert Kraft’s demand of dropping rapper Macklemore, an unabashed Palestine supporter, from his North American tour, he did not expect to hit a discordant note. But now it’s the 35-year-old British singer who is facing boycott calls. Several supporting acts have walked away from the tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Other musicians, led by Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters, have panned Sheeran online. Meanwhile, hundreds of musicians have joined the No Music for Genocide initiative in recent months to bar their catalogues from being played in Israel. To limit the PR damage, the British pop artist has donated to Palestinian causes. But having missed the new beat the world is increasingly jiving to, Sheeran may never be able to get back in rhythm..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Asatya lurks
editorials.passage:
The story so far: The tragic collapse of an illegal, muti-storied PG accommodation in New Delhi, which claimed the lives of seven young people and left several others seriously injured, has understandably triggered widespread public outrage. Print, electronic and social media are resounding with reports, debates, discussions, op-eds and, predictably, politically coloured statements. The arrests of the owners of the killer structure are necessary and welcome, but insufficient as a remedial response; especially if such tragedies are not to recur. 

“Greedy for rental income, owners built extra floors,” reads one headline. Perhaps the larger point we are missing is this: it is not the greed of the PG owners alone that caused the tragedy; it is the product of a greedy system operating under the colluding eyes of those whose duty it was to prevent tragedies of this kind. Bigger point: If the discussion centers on illegal construction, negligence, arrests and compensation alone, we will miss the forest for the trees. The collapse of the building is only the visible manifestation of a much deeper crisis: the criminal neglect of education, not just in NCR but country-wide, and the failure to provide safe, adequate and affordable accommodation for students. 

And this, not because we lacked the required resources, but because we value money above life. The resultant tragic loss of lives must be seen as human sacrifices made at the altar of the God of Greed. Thanks to be scandalous failure of our education enterprise nationally, Delhi has become an educational refuge for young people from across India. About 50 per cent of the 700,000 students enrolled in DU colleges are from other states. Each one of them, numbering some 350,000, needs accommodation. The infrastructure available to accommodate them is woefully inadequate. Such a state of affairs serves as a goldmine for PG accommodation sharks, who are rich enough to grease the palms of those in authority. 

The abysmal demand-supply shortfall forces our young students to risk their life for the sake of education, precisely because the option to be safe doesn’t exist for them. This is a national shame. This problem is not unique to Delhi. In varying degrees it prevails in our cities and metropolises. Given the above, the untimely death of the seven students in the Satya Niketan tragedy cannot be classified as an accident. It is a predictable by-product of greed-induced systemic failure that countenanced human lives being gambled with to make a big, quick buck. Here’s the question that stares us in the face from this tragedy: Why do so many young Indians have to flock to Delhi, leaving their home states in search of better educational opportunities? 

Surely, such educational migrations are not natural. They happen nonetheless, like water going uphill when pumped. The pump in this case is the scandalous state of education at all levels throughout the country; in particular, of higher education. Many of these students cannot afford living and studying in Delhi. Parents strain their economic resources to the utmost, just because educating their children is their top-most priority. It devastates them to have their children return home dead. And this brings us to an uncomfortable question: Why is education so grossly neglected? 

It cannot be because India’s ruling class does not understand its value. When it comes to their own children our ruling elite are keen to provide the best quality education in the most expensive and prestigious universities in the West. They ensure that their much-cherished children do not suffer the least inconvenience in any way. The disparity is stark. Education is valued enormously for one’s own children, yet millions of other young Indians are left to struggle with substandard education in poorly-run, ill-equipped institutions, and unsafe living conditions. 

This is not ignorance. It is criminal neglect. The more you regard it, the less accidental it looks. Look closer, and you will see lineaments of barely camouflaged intentions. Our education system is what it is, not because we lack the political will to educate our children and youths, but because there is a will to patronize the vested interests thriving through this scandalous state of affairs. To understand the above, the story of St. Stephen’s College is worth recalling. Founded in 1881 by five Cambridge missionaries, the college was established at a time when educational opportunities in Delhi were extremely limited, particularly for the poor. 

The founders had very modest resources. Yet they believed that there was no better way to love a people than to provide educational opportunities to them. To them, education was an outworking of love. If we love, we will respect the worth of the people we love. This activates vigilance in caring for them. To care is not only to preserve the current worth, but also to enhance it, as every parent knows. Education is the best means for enhancing the worth of individuals and nations. The founders of St. Stephen’s College were animated by a spirit of selfless love ~ the belief that those who are less privileged deserve not less, but greater care, attention and opportunity. That idea seems to have been lost somewhere along the way. 

The St. Stephen’s story further reveals the extraordinary demand for quality education. The college has only around 400 undergraduate seats, while tens of thousands of students applied. The tragedy was that many of those rejected were among the brightest young people in the country ~ not because they lacked merit, but simply because there was no room for them. Permission was sought to expand the intake in Economics and to introduce Political Science (Hon.). Adequate library and infrastructure facilities were available. Only a limited number of additional teaching posts had to be sanctioned. Yet despite repeated efforts, the necessary permissions never came. 

The prospect of some hundred more young men and women benefiting from quality higher education did not appeal to the ‘competent’ authorities. It is far easier to run an illicit PG facility that could kill many an inmate, provided the relevant authorities see scope for ‘additional mobilisation of personal resources’ in it. Such an experience is not limited to St. Stephen’s. The larger truth it exposes is that India has failed to expand educational opportunity ~ not because the resources were lacking, but because our patriotism falls short of loving the people. We profess, but do not practise, love. At its deepest level, education must not be deemed an industry, a degree-producing mechanism or a speculative investment. 

It is a domain of public service ~ a sacred enterprise in human development. To care for the learner is first to recognise their worth and then to do everything possible to enhance it. Where this concern is absent, education risks becoming an industry rather than an investment in human development. This is why the Delhi incident should force us to ask not merely who violated building regulations, but what kind of society allows young people to live in dangerous conditions simply because they have nowhere else to go, or afford safer roofs over their heads. The answer cannot be found only in courts, commissions or administrative inquiries. Those institutions provide temporary justice and relief, but the deeper transformation must come from society itself. 

The purpose of education should be to equip young people with knowledge and skills that enable them to solve the problems of their society, as Plato envisaged in The Republic. Education, therefore, should nurture citizens who hold themselves responsible for others ~ not merely seek personal advancement. The distinction can be expressed simply: missionary or mercenary. A missionary serves because he or she loves the people and cares for them. A mercenary has his eyes fixed on what he can get out of the people, unmindful of their safety and welfare. 

As Shakespeare says, in serving them, he serves only himself. If education produces increasingly mercenary citizens ~ people trained only to milk and massage the system to their advantage, no matter at what cost to others ~ society loses its developmental momentum and moral vitality. The seven young lives lost in Delhi should therefore not become a media will-o'-the-wisp that glows and vanishes from public attention. 

Their sacrifice should compel us to confront the larger failures: inadequate educational infrastructure, unsafe accommodation, corruption, administrative indifference, and the cynical choice to keep the common man in a fool’s paradise, anaesthetised to his real condition by the hypnotic power of propaganda-driven media. The real question is not simply why or how the building collapsed on our children? It is this: What kind of society forces young people to risk their lives merely to pursue their dreams? Until we answer that question ~ and act upon the answers that emerge ~ we may have, God forbid, a procession of Satya Niketan heartbreaks 

(The writers, both authors, are, respectively, former Principal, St. Stephen’s College, Delhi, and former General Manager, International Centre Goa)

editorials.title: It costs a lot to seek a public job
editorials.passage:
A public job is advertised. Before you may b e considered for it, you must pay. The people applying are, by definition, the people without an income. Nobody in the government seems to find this odd. Start with the logic, because the logic is indefensible before a single figure is quoted. The state advertises a vacancy. It then requires, as a precondition of even being looked at, a payment from the applicant. 

The entire pool of applicants consists of people who do not have the job in question, and most of whom do not have any job at all. That is why they are applying. So, the one group in society guaranteed to have the least money is the group from which the state has decided to collect money before it will do anything. This is not a subtle injustice requiring careful excavation. It is visible on the face of every advertisement, and it survives only because we have stopped looking at it. 

A fee buys a service. This one buys a chance. Uttar Pradesh's provincial services examination in 2024 drew roughly 5.7 lakh applicants for 220 posts. Bihar's 67th combined examination drew 5.5 lakh for 803. In any such competition, upwards of 99 per cent of the money collected comes from people who will receive nothing whatsoever in return. Whatever is being sold here, it is not a service. It is closer to a lottery ticket, sold by the state, priced by the state, and drawn at the state's convenience. The price bears no relation to the cost. The Union Public Service Commission processes applications for the Civil Services Examination at Rs 100. 

The Staff Selection Commission runs the Combined Graduate Level examination on the same Rs 100. These are the largest and most complex recruitment exercises anywhere in the country. That single number refutes every cost-recovery claim made beneath it. If the Union of India can register, scrutinise, admit and examine a candidate for the IAS at Rs 100, no state commission needs Rs 800 and no university needs Rs 1,500 to do the same for a clerk's post or a contract lectureship. The gap between Rs 100 and Rs 1,500 is not a cost. It is a mark-up, and it is charged to the unemployed. 

The money is taken before the state commits to doing anything. Around a crore candidates paid Rs 500 each for a Railway Recruitment Board notification in 2019 and then waited more than a thousand days for an examination. Delhi University's non-teaching recruitment, notified in February 2021, still had not produced an examination when its staff union demanded an inquiry this August. On 18 August the Jharkhand government cancelled an entire series of recruitment processes conducted since 2014. Not one of these produced a refund. The fee is collected on the day of advertisement; nothing at all is owed if the recruitment stalls, collapses or is annulled a decade later. 

Delay costs the recruiter nothing. Abandonment costs the recruiter nothing. The only component of the process that never fails is the payment gateway. And it compounds. Madhya Pradesh bills separately at prelims and again at Mains. Several recruiters demand a fresh fee for each post applied for, even where the candidate holds a single registration number. And when a cancelled process is revived, the meter resets: Lucknow University advertised ten contractual law teaching posts in November 2023, cancelle d that ro und, re-advertised the identical posts this August, and informed earlier applicants that they must apply afresh. They paid in 2023, waited thre e ye ars, and re ceive d no appointment, no refund and a second invoice. 

A diligent candidate applying to fifteen vacancies in a year, at Rs 800 or Rs 1,000 apiece, is sp ending more than many households in the state earn in a month. The harder you look for work, the more you are charged for looking. Where relief does exist, it is attached to the wrong variable. At the UPSC and the SSC, women, SC, ST and disabled candidates pay no thing. A candidate in the Economically Weaker Section pays the full amount, exactly what a General or OBC candidate pays. State advertisements repeat the pattern faithfully: Lucknow University's law recruitment this August set Rs 1,500 for unreserved, OBC and EWS applicants alike, and Rs 1,200 for SC and ST. 

Consider what that arrangement actually says. EWS is the one category in Indian public employment defined purely and explicitly by money, a family income below Rs 8 lakh a year, certified by the state's own revenue machiner y. It is, by construction, the category of applicants least able to pay. It is also the only major category granted no fee relief at all. The relief that does exist, meanwhile, carries no income test of any kind, so a candidate from a prosperous household pays a fraction of what a genuinely poor EWS applicant pays, or nothing. Whatever one's view of reservation in selection, a fee waiver is a different question and should be answered differently. 

Selection preferences are defende d on grounds of representation and historical exclusion, and that argument can be had on its own terms. A waiver turns on one thing only: whether this person can find Rs 1,500 this month. That is a question about a bank balance, and it has an obvious test. The state already operates that test, since it certifies the Rs 8 lakh EWS ceiling itself. If the machinery is trusted to allocate ten per cent of all public jobs, it can be trusted to decide who pays Rs 1,000 to apply for one. Waive the fee by income, for anyone below the line, whatever their category. The remedies are neither radical nor expensive. Cap recruitment fees at the Rs 100 the Union itself manages on. Waive them on proof of income rather than category. 

Charge once per recruitment, not once per post and again at every stage. Refund or carry forward automatically wherever a process is cancelled or left unconcluded beyond a fixed period. And require every recruiting body to publish what it collected and what it spent. None of this requires a new idea. It requires only that somebody in authority re ad one of these advertisements and notice what it says: that in a country arguing endlessly about jobs, the state has arranged matters so that the one transaction it completes promptly, reliably and without exception is taking money from people who do not have one. 

(The writer is a retired employee of the Uttar Pradesh government)

editorials.title: Gen Z angst on the rise in Odisha
editorials.passage:
When young voices gathered at Jantar Mantar recently to demand accountability and fair recruitment, the spark resonated far beyond the national capital. For the youth of Odisha, that wave of student assertion hits close to home. An entire generation in the state is currently caught in a tiring loop of administrative blunders, delayed recruitment notifications, and legal deadlocks. What was supposed to be a journey of higher learning and career building has turned into a test of survival. 

Look at the sheer number of roadblocks hitting a young candidate in Odisha today. The Sub-Inspector recruitment exams have been rocked by scam allegations. The Revenue Inspector examination, handed over to controversial testing agencies, faced severe technical glitches that ruined months of hard preparation for thousands of rural aspirants. For those aiming at academia and teaching careers, the wait is even more agonizing. Even for university gold medallists, NET qualifiers, and Ph.D. scholars who have proven their academic merit, the path forward is blocked by procedural paralysis. The State Selection Board lecturer recruitment has been stuck in court for over two years, leaving qualified candidates waiting date after date while state colleges run with massive faculty shortages. 

Similarly, thousands of teaching aspirants find themselves stuck due to legal and administrative delays surrounding the Leave Training Reserve (LTR) teacher recruitment process. Compounding these issues, the National Council for Teacher Education recently issued show-cause notices to 15 B.Ed colleges across Odisha over alleged illegal faculty appointments and eligibility violations. When teacher training institutes themselves fail basic compliance, what kind of educators are we preparing for the future? This carelessness is not limited to higher education, as it starts right in school. 

The recent disclosure of 1,678 factual errors in state school textbooks showed how deeply quality control has slipped. From primary school books to university recruitment, administrative apathy seems to be the common thread running through the system. Even when the government tries to modernize, the execution burdens the students. The state launched a unified HIMS portal for faculty recruitment across universities, which was supposed to simplify applications. Yet, an applicant applying to four different universities through the exact same portal is forced to pay separate, heavy application fees for each institution. Adding to the frustration is the practice of re-engaging retired faculty members. 

While thousands of NET and Ph.D. qualified young scholars sit unemployed, re-hiring retired professors closes doors for the next generation. Despite these hurdles, Odisha's youth are beginning to push back. At VSSUT in Burla, students raised their voices against rigid uniform rules that felt disconnected from a modern engineering campus. Across the state, aggrieved aspirants of LTR teacher recruitment and other stalled exams are taking to digital platforms and street demonstrations to demand swift court resolutions and fair recruitment schedules. These are not isolated protests, as they show a growing refusal among students to accept administrative inefficiency as normal. 

There is also a glaring contradiction in state policy. While the government's fee waiver scheme from KG to PG is a welcome initiative on paper, the ground reality for self-financing courses tells a different story. Students in these programmes continue to pay exorbitant admission and development fees, turning higher education into a costly burden for middle class families. This brings us to a crucial turning point. As recruitment scams, court stays, and administrative flaws pile up, the question is no longer just about fixing individual exams. 

It is about the future of Odisha's youth. Will Gen Z need an intellectual revolution by building a clear, organized demand for transparency, digitized exam governance, and merit-based hiring before a real change can happen on the ground? Or will the youth allow these systemic failures to quietly pass by? The answer to that question will decide not just the fate of our campuses, but the future of the state itself. 

(The writer is a Gen Z scholar and a gold medallist in MA Political Science from the Central University of Punjab)

editorials.title: Tata’s Test
editorials.passage:
The struggle over the leadership of Tata Sons is more than a disagreement about the tenure of a chairman. It is a test of whether one of India’s most influential business groups can reconcile concentrated ownership, professional management and institutional accountability without undermining the stability on which its reputation rests. N Chandrasekaran’s continuation for another five years offers the Tata Group leadership continuity at a consequential moment. But the opposition of Noel Tata, chairman of Tata Trusts, exposes a fundamental disagreement over who has the authority to determine the group’s direction. 

The question is significant because Tata Trusts owns 66 per cent of Tata Sons, the holding company at the centre of the conglomerate. The dispute highlights a structural tension in the Tata model. Its charitable trusts provide the group with a distinctive institutional identity, linking commercial success with philanthropic objectives. Yet the same arrangement places enormous influence in the hands of trustees whose responsibilities extend beyond ordinary shareholder interests. When those responsibilities collide with the decisions of professional management, the consequences can reach far beyond the boardroom. The immediate concern is the legitimacy of the reappointment. 

Noel Tata has argued that the decision is invalid because it lacked the necessary support from the Trusts’ nominees under the company’s articles of association. The board’s decision and the objections to it now create uncertainty over the governance process itself. Such a dispute cannot be resolved merely by asserting the authority of either the chairman or the majority shareholder. It requires a clear determination of the applicable rules and their consistent observance. The timing makes the disagreement particularly consequential. Tata Sons has agreed to comply with the Reserve Bank of India’s directive requiring it to pursue a listing, after the regulator rejected its application to deregister as a non-banking financial company. 

The proposed transition could reshape the relationship between the holding company, its shareholders and the wider group. It also raises questions about transparency, accountability and the future exercise of shareholder control. A listing would not automatically settle the underlying conflict. Nor would it necessarily diminish the influence of Tata Trusts. But it could bring greater scrutiny to a corporate structure that has historically combined private ownership with substantial public visibility and philanthropic responsibility. For Chandrasekaran, the challenge is therefore larger than managing a sprawling business empire. 

He must lead through a period in which the authority of the board itself is contested. For Noel Tata and the trusts, the responsibility is equally significant: safeguarding their institutional role while ensuring that governance disagreements do not destabilise the businesses that sustain their philanthropic mission. The Tata Group’s reputation has been built over generations, but reputation cannot substitute for sound governance. Its future depends on establishing a transparent, legally defensible framework in which ownership rights, board responsibilities and management authority are clearly reconciled. The chairman’s tenure may have been extended, but the more consequential test is whether the institution can resolve its differences without compromising the confidence on which its legacy rests

editorials.title: Dangerous Waters
editorials.passage:
The collision between Indian and Pakistani naval vessels in the Arabian Sea raises a question that extends beyond the immediate dispute over responsibility: how secure is the fragile peace between two nuclear-armed neighbours when even routine military operations can become sources of confrontation? More than a year after India and Pakistan exchanged military strikes before agreeing to a ceasefire, the incident exposes the limitations of a peace sustained without a corresponding restoration of trust. 

The diplomatic engagements initiated by India in Delhi and Islamabad demonstrate how quickly a maritime encounter can acquire political significance. Yet diplomatic protests, however strongly worded, cannot substitute for mechanisms that prevent such encounters from escalating. The 1991 agreement on advance notification of military exercises, manoeuvres and troop movements reflects an important recognition: military preparedness need not inevitably produce confrontation if each side understands the other's intentions. Its provisions governing the proximity of naval vessels in international waters are particularly relevant when warships operate in an environment where miscalculation can have consequences far beyond the immediate encounter. 

Both countries have accused the other of disregarding these safeguards. India has challenged the conduct of the Pakistani naval unit, while Pakistan has alleged that an Indian vessel behaved aggressively during its SEASPARK-26 exercise. These competing accounts cannot independently establish culpability. What matters now is whether the circumstances can be examined objectively, rather than allowing mutual accusations to become another entrenched grievance. 

The danger is that the incident could become part of a larger cycle in which every military encounter reinforces suspicion. In such an atmosphere, even a relatively minor maritime incident may invite disproportionate responses, particularly when domestic political pressures reward displays of resolve. The resulting escalation need not begin with a deliberate decision to wage war; it could emerge through successive misjudgements and retaliatory actions. There is also a wider strategic dimension. The Arabian Sea is an important corridor for international commerce and energy supplies. Instability between India and Pakistan would carry consequences beyond their bilateral relationship, affecting confidence in regional security and the predictability of maritime operations. 

Neither country needs to abandon its security requirements to recognise these risks. India and Pakistan can maintain military readiness while strengthening communication between naval commands, ensuring compliance with existing agreements and establishing procedures for promptly investigating potentially dangerous encounters. Such arrangements are not concessions to the other side but practical safeguards against unintended conflict. The central challenge is to prevent the ceasefire from becoming merely an interval between confrontations. 

Peace cannot depend entirely on the absence of another major military exchange. It must also be sustained through disciplined conduct, credible communication and the capacity to manage disagreements without allowing them to spiral. The collision should therefore prompt more than another exchange of diplomatic protests. It should compel both governments to examine whether their existing arrangements are sufficient to keep military operations from producing a crisis. When the consequences of miscalculation could be grave, restraint is not weakness. It is an indispensable instrument of national security

editorials.title: Kiltartan’s poor
editorials.passage:
As I write this, the first ministers of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales are coordinating moves to ask for referendums to be held in their respective regions on separation from the United Kingdom. The demand is not new, but this time the fact that it is being raised by the government leaders in those places makes it important. And it brings to mind one work from the most famous poet of Irish descent.

One hundred years ago, in 1926, William Butler Yeats was a little over 60. The Nobel Prize for Literature had come to him three years earlier.

What occupied him that year, however, was something that is not widely known outside the world of the Yeats-smitten. Nominated to the Senate in 1922 (a year before the Nobel Prize) by the newly constituted Irish Free State, Yeats held a public office. Yeats in a sarkari job? Indeed, yes. He chaired a Senate Committee to help identify the new nation’s coins. This was not a routine thing. The matter had, for Ireland, great cultural, social and political ramifications.

Yeats, himself born to Protestant parents, wanted the coins to be acceptable to Ireland’s Protestant north and its Catholic south. More specifically, he wanted the coins to not bear any religious image or connotation whatsoever and, more, to be “elegant, racy of the soil and utterly unpolitical”. Yeats’ clarity of intent led the Committee to choose the Irish harp for the coin’s face. The Irish harp, or cláirseach , had a history spanning over a thousand years and had appeared in Irish life since at least the 8th to the 10th centuries, harpists holding a high status as valued musicians, historians, and storytellers. Imagine what would have resulted in terms of religious discord if nascent India had been asked to choose for its national emblem among theocratically-driven symbols comprising crescents, crosses, swastikas , trishuls , swords!

Yeats’ choice for the coin design has to be seen with the thought underlying his poem, “An Irish Airman Foresees His Death”. The poem emphatically rejects nationalistic super-egos. Its redefinition of ‘country’ and ‘countrymen’ rings not one but a whole string of bells when Yeats, in the voice of the Irish Airman, says (not Ireland but) “ My country is Kiltartan Cross. ”

Kiltartan Cross being a point in Galway, Ireland, he triggers for us the question, ‘What is ‘country’, what is ‘ desh ’?’ ‘ Desh ’ is, for any Indian, India that is Bharat. But what is it that makes that Desh , with its capital D, one’s very own desh , the place one belongs to and which is one’s very own? A map, a slogan? It is places, particular places and particular people. Speaking for myself, Delhi, where I was born and schooled and went to college in, is my desh . Because the old Hindustan Times building opposite Scindia House in Connaught Circus, where I spent the first twenty-two years of my life, is Delhi. As are the red-brick buildings of Modern School on Barakhamba Road and St Stephens College along the old ridge, for me, Delhi. And Fort St George by the sea on Madras’ Marina, where I worked as a cub civil servant, is, for me, Madras. Take these away, and what can remain of my desh in these venues? Nothing! My desh is my desh because of the many desh -s, the many Kiltartan Cross-s, in it. A closeness makes one’s ‘country’, a belonging does, a feeling of immediacy that says ‘this place, this spot, is mine, it is me…’ — as in being ‘one with’. One with a particular patch of earth, one with an ecology of shared experiencing.

And when Yeats says, “ My countrymen Kiltartan’s poor ”, what is he saying? Fellow countrymen are not names on a sheet of the same list but a fellowship in the same ecology of being and belonging. Nor are ‘my people’ necessarily kin. People are the samaj they make up.

In Bombay, where, as a kid, I went almost every year in the summer vacations, an old rafuwala , or darner, used to walk down our road, Alexandra Road, in leafy Gamdevi, calling out “ rafuwaalaa-en rafuwaala-en ”, the very nasal ‘ en ’ ending having no sanction in syntax or grammar but great traction in communication. The little café in my old college in Delhi had two waiters, Dolly and Shelley. They were, for us, not waiters in the café but the café itself where they served us ‘crumbled’ (scrambled) eggs and ‘buttar toast’. Just outside that café sat, on the ground, quirky Sukhia, the seller of pedas and samosas stacked in a wooden dabba with a creaky lid. These were my Kiltartan’s fellow citizens. Likewise, in Madras, my mother’s driver, Mubarak, a youth from South Arcot’s town called Lalpettai, was for her, and for me, the human equivalent of Madras’ warmth. As was, later, for my wife and me, the vendor of greens who would come every day pushing his cart and intoning his call, ‘ Keerai , Keerai, Keerai ’, in three ascending tones. Years later, my wife and I were walking down to Lebang, in the Darjeeling hills, when we came across two handsome youths carrying on their shoulders dhunkis , the wooden mattress fluffer that makes the most beautiful twangy sound when used. I asked them where they were from, for they looked like they did not belong to those hills. They were from Chhapra in Bihar, they said; their names were Nizamuddin and Firoz. They reminded me of the great chaupai from Tulsidas in Raga Kamod about Rama and Lakshmana that Pandit Kumar Gandharva used to sing — “ dou bhraataa/ loka lochana sukha daataa ” (the brothers two/ giving happiness to beholding eyes). They said they walked over large areas in the hills in order to fluff razais (quilts), charging Rs 85 for doing an old razai and Rs 550 for making a new one. These two were migrant workers, not of the kind that wander unemployed looking for any job, but skilled men with a skill to use and create work from.

Not ‘public laws’ (Yeats’ phrase) but personal bondings made and make our desh . And simple folk, not necessarily fellow rolls-men, our countrymen. Take those people away from any place that I think of as mine and that place loses its life.

The Special Intensive Revision that is trimming electoral lists across the country, deleting lakhs upon lakhs of individuals from them, the former election commissioner, Ashok Lavasa, said the other day, is legal under the law. But he says it is “definitely not fair” to millions of citizens. Delivering the Jagdeep Singh Chhokar Memorial Lecture organised by the Association for Democratic Reforms, Lavasa brought to my mind Yeats’ line, “ My countrymen Kiltartan’s poor. ”

Will Delimitation turn our Kiltartan Cross-s from being places where humans live into neat diagrams with so many dots per so many heads? Will the SIR’s operations think of our countrymen as the equivalents of ‘Kiltartan’s poor’? Or as weeds in a garden of its arboreal imagination?

As the United Kingdom ponders the concerns of the three first ministers in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, let us reflect on the legacies India and Ireland share in winning and protecting freedom.

editorials.title: BJP’s social media diktat puts its old guard under the camera’s spotlight
editorials.passage:
In the Bharatiya Janata Party’s new-age political grammar, it is no longer enough to act — the action must also be seen on social media. But this has made some of the party’s old-timers uncomfortable. They are being nudged to remain active on social media. The Union defence minister, Rajnath Singh, had a particularly busy day on September 17, the birthday of the prime minister, Narendra Modi. His morning began at the Kashi Vishwanath temple in Varanasi, where he led a special puja for Modi’s long life. Sitting in the sanctum sanctorum with the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, Yogi Adityanath, the CM of Andhra Pradesh, N. Chandrababu Naidu, and the Union food processing industries minister, Chirag Paswan, Singh kept his hands folded as priests chanted mantras. He then addressed BJP workers and flagged off a bike rally from Varanasi to Vadnagar, Modi’s birthplace, to mark 25 years of the PM in public life. Back in Delhi, Singh joined the ‘Ashirwad ka Diya’ event in the evening. And, as the new party diktat demands, every stop had to find its way onto social media. The accompanying X video perhaps said more than the words. The 75-year-old Singh appeared visibly uneasy holding the earthen lamp before the camera and delivering his message: a prayer for Modi’s “excellent health and long life”.

A year on, the pull of the singer-composer, Zubeen Garg, and his songs has only grown stronger. The presence of thousands cutting across age, class, profession at his memorial site in Guwahati on his first death anniversary is proof of this. Political parties and politicians who mostly disagree with each other were also active, physically and on social media, to honour Garg and his contributions. The ruling BJP organised a day-long blood donation camp, Jibon Xurobhi, across the state. The Opposition Congress, too, observed “Zubeen Garg Smriti Sandhya” in memory of the artist, including lighting diyas and taking out peaceful processions. Garg clearly seems to have united the state.

The PM’s 76th birthday gave BJP leaders in Odisha a chance to show their unflinching loyalty to Narendra Modi. Leaders ranging from the CM, Mohan Charan Majhi, to senior BJP leaders like the former Union minister, Dilip Ray, visited temples and lit ashirwad ka diyas for Modi’s health and well-being. All the leaders went to temples, lit diyas , and posted photos on social media. Ray, who recently drew the wrath of the Union minister, Jual Oram, posted a video of himself lighting a diya for the PM, signalling that he remained close to Modi. Even Majhi lit a diya at the famous Mukteswar Temple in Bhubaneswar, where ove 11,000 diyas were illuminated in his presence. The CM’s office claimed that around one crore diyas were lit across the state. Majhi also penned a tribute to Modi’s leadership, which was widely published in vernacular newspapers. The former Union minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, quietly went to the Samaleswari Temple in Sambalpur and lit a diya for Modi’s health and a blessed life.

Buoyed by the success of Operation Toofan — an anti-narcotics campaign launched by the Keralam government after he took over as home minister — Ramesh Chennithala has now constituted an Anti-Narcotics Investigation Team with immediate effect. Chennithala came up with this significant decision after Operation Toofan saw 10,918 cases being registered and 11,776 people getting arrested under the drive in the less than four months the Congress-led United Democratic Front government has been in office. The newly constituted ANIT will strengthen Operation Toofan and also target high-value narcotic cases and help identify the kingpins of drug trafficking, major gang members and narcotic sources at a time when drug addiction and substance abuse has become a cause of concern in the state.

Candidates for the Delhi Univer­sity Students’ Union — India’s largest directly elected students’ union — have turned even the most embarrassing stones to attract voters. The Congress-backed National Students’ Union of India candidate got the endorsement of the internet medicine man, Pradeep Dhaka, who claims to have a panacea for diabetes and is known for his videos in flashy cars. Dhaka appears in the campaign video with wads of cash around him asking students to vote for the NSUI vice-presidential candidate, Vir Chatrath, and that he will give his diabetes medicine’s lifetime supply for free to supporters. The Aam Aadmi Party student-wing, Association of Students for Alternative Politics, put up a poster of the actor, Pankaj Tripathi, to seek votes for their secretary candidate, Pankaj Kumar.

editorials.title: Letters to the editor: Ig Nobels remind us that curiosity and laughter remain achievements worth honouring in themselves
editorials.passage:
Sir — The 2026 Ig Nobel Prizes are a welcome antidote to the self-importance surrounding their illustrious counterparts. This year’s winners of the Ig Nobel Prizes studied the obnoxiousness of the rich, designed a splashless urinal, examined friendships sustained by mutual enemies, and discovered the remarkable energy content of cockroach milk. Such research may appear frivolous. Yet, amidst war, inequality, authoritarianism, climate anxiety and the fear of machines, the Ig Nobels remind us that curiosity and laughter remain achievements worth honouring in themselves.

Sir — The decision of the Election Commission of India to freeze the party name, Trinamool Congress, and its floral symbol amid a factional dispute highlights a troubling legal gap (“Black day, will fight: Mamata”, Sept 19). Clear legislation could establish the principles to resolve rival claims to party names and symbols. Yet, an overly broad law may invite political interference. Regular, transparent, inner-party elections offer a better solution: they can determine which faction commands legitimate support and reduce dependence on piecemeal precedents.

Sir — Political friction has intensified in West Bengal ahead of the October 6 assembly bypolls. The Nandigram candidate of the Mamata All India Trinamool Congress withdrew her nomination after meeting the Bharatiya Janata Party chief minister. Its Rejinagar nominee briefly announced his withdrawal before reversing course. Mamata Banerjee called the developments a “black day for democracy”, alleged intimidation and accused party rebels of acting as the BJP’s “A-team” (“BJP Nandigram rival shrinks”, Sept 19). The episodes reveal the organisational disarray confronting her faction after its assembly-election defeat.

Sir — The arrest of the Congress candidate for the Nandigram bypolls, Milan Pradhan, in connection with cases arising from the 2007 Nandigram agitation came hours after Mamata Banerjee announced her support for him. The Congress and Banerjee’s faction of the Trinamool Congress have alleged political vendetta. But an arrest alone does not disqualify a candidate: Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act links disqualification to conviction and the sentence imposed. The timing of his arrest still warrants scrutiny.

Sir — The everyday heroes that Srimoyee Bagchi writes about in “Heroic shades” (Sept 18) are nowhere to be found in India — most such heroes have been killed, jailed or intimidated into silence. The tragedy is that unlike Gotham, where a billionaire had the moral courage to save the city, India’s rich are complicit in its downward trajectory.

Sir — As Batman reacts to the complex struggles of society, he strays from the traditional definition of what it means to be a hero, attempting to deal with shifting forms of evil. As a human, he inevitably makes mistakes, and his actions in his position of power must bear scrutiny. In spite of his flaws, however, Batman is able to confront the worst face of Gotham without giving up on hope and in that lies his heroism.

Aditya Mukherjee, Calcutta

Sir — The government’s messaging increasingly resembles a comic politician on TV attempting to reassure Gotham’s residents while the city burns. Unfortunately, there is no Batman in sight for Indians.

Harsh Pawaria, Rohtak, Haryana

editorials.title: Friends in deed: Editorial on France’s move to give friendship legal recognition
editorials.passage:
Should the blood of the covenant be thicker than the water of the womb? Clémence Guetté, a parliamentarian from the French radical-left party, La France Insoumise, has given this adage political substance by seeking for friends the legal rights that are now reserved for families; these include caregiver and bereavement leave, access to public housing and inheritance. Her proposal challenges what the philosopher, Elizabeth Brake, termed as ‘amatonormativity’ — the assumption that a romantic partnership is the natural centre of adult life and, therefore, deserves greater recognition than other intimate bonds. The same hierarchy governs the law, which accords automatic importance to relationships created by marriage or birth while treating friendship as socially valuable but legally inconsequential. Yet, friendship is often the more consequential bond, sustained by affinity, trust and freely assumed obligations. As marriage rates decline across the world, childlessness increases and more people choose to live alone, the distance between this legal hierarchy and the organisation of actual lives is becoming harder to defend.

That distance has material consequences. A friend may provide care during illness, manage a household and arrange a funeral, yet he or she often possesses no standing before a hospital, employer or housing authority. In India, even the official nomination of a friend for a bank account or insurance policy may not override the claims of legal heirs. Four years ago, the Supreme Court’s recognition that “atypical families” are as real as traditional ones and equally deserving of legal protection provides a basis for similar legal reform in this country. Precedents already exist in other nations: some Canadian caregiving provisions recognise a person considered “like family”, while Hawaii permits adults to register as reciprocal beneficiaries for specified rights. Law could likewise include a nominated friend within the definition of kin for medical access, emergency decisions, leave, tenancy succession and funeral arrangements.

However, a word of caution is necessary. Such recognition need not convert friendship into a legal contract. A declaration naming a friend for particular purposes, capable of amendment or withdrawal, would be sufficient. Rights involving inheritance, pensions or public housing would require safeguards against fraud and conflicting claims, but these administrative difficulties do not justify excluding chosen relationships altogether. The greater danger lies in allowing recognition to become regulation. The Uniform Civil Code passed in some Indian states, which requires the registration of live-in relationships, shows how easily ‘reform’ can enable surveillance of private life. The State should neither investigate the intimacy or duration of a friendship nor judge its authenticity. Friendship derives its ethical significance from obligations that are freely assumed rather than imposed by descent or convention. A liberal law should respect the consequences of that choice without seeking authority over the affection behind it. The purpose of change must be to enlarge personal autonomy, not to place another private relationship under official supervision.

editorials.title: Trump’s Iran sanctions have a China problem
editorials.passage:
In late August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared an “economic D-Day” against Iran, promising “the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary.” The D-Day analogy is an odd one for a campaign whose success ultimately depends on China, an American ally at Normandy but a strategic rival today.

For the Trump administration’s “zero-leakage” policy to succeed, foreign financial institutions would need to monitor and police their own customers. And there is no way to achieve the “total isolation” of the Iranian regime without Chinese banks doing much of the hard work of sanctions enforcement.

Before the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the US Treasury estimated that China purchased roughly 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports. Years of sanctions have already pushed much of the Iranian oil trade into an alternative system capable of operating without the dollar, the SWIFT interbank payments platform, and the correspondent banks that have long given the United States its financial leverage.

Much of this trade moves through Iran’s rahbar shadow-banking system, which according to the Treasury processes “tens of billions of dollars” worth of trade each year, “much of it derived from Iran’s overseas sales of oil and petrochemicals.” Today, Iran settles those sales primarily in renminbi.

Secondary US sanctions have previously changed the behaviour of major Chinese banks even when China officially rejected them. Within the first week of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, for example, the offshore units of the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) stopped issuing dollar-denominated letters of credit for purchases of physical Russian commodities. Renminbi-denominated credit lines remained available for some customers but required senior management approval. The Bank of China (BOC) restricted financing for Russian commodities, while its Singapore branch went even further and ceased financing transactions involving Russian companies and oil.

But China’s largest banks — its policy banks and the “big four” state-owned commercial banks, the ICBC, the BOC, the China Construction Bank, and the Agricultural Bank of China — are not America’s hardest enforcement problem. Their global operations require them to maintain access to dollar liquidity and correspondent banking relationships, which are far more valuable than any business with sanctioned Iranian entities. This dependence on the global dollar system gives them powerful incentives to limit their exposure to US sanctions. As former Treasury Secretary Janet L. Yellen observed, China’s large banks “are not banks that we most need to worry about” as they “really, really value their correspondent-banking relations.”

The greater challenge lies deeper within the Chinese financial system, among thousands of smaller regional banks with far less exposure to the dollar-based system and therefore less to lose if that access is cut off. In 2023, the People’s Bank of China counted more than 3,800 urban and rural banks and credit cooperatives, in addition to private banks and other institutions. In 2024, as the US threatened Chinese banks with secondary sanctions, Russian companies increasingly turned to smaller regional institutions with minimal ties to Western markets.

The real question facing the Trump administration is whether it can compel or induce smaller Chinese banks to scrutinize customers and transactions deliberately structured to conceal Iranian connections — and refuse the business once they uncover them. Iran’s rahbars use foreign-exchange houses, layers of offshore shell companies, and bank accounts in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, and Singapore to move oil proceeds on behalf of sanctioned Iranian entities.

Chinese buyers of Iranian crude, especially independent “teapot” refiners in Shandong, which have absorbed most of the sanctioned oil, do not need to send money to an Iranian bank. A buyer can simply pay an offshore front company in renminbi. The money can then be used to pay Chinese suppliers on Iran’s behalf or sent elsewhere.

On paper, the transaction may have no connection to Iran. To the Chinese bank processing the payment, it could look like an ordinary transfer from a Hong Kong trading firm to a company in Dubai. Internal records from the Iranian exchange house Radin, for example, identified dozens of China-based front companies maintaining accounts at Chinese banks. FinCEN has similarly documented transactions operated by Hong Kong-based shell companies that it linked to Iran’s shadow-banking network.

This makes compliance much harder. Instead of simply refusing to do business with sanctioned entities, banks now have to uncover hidden links to Iran in accounts and transactions where no Iranian name appears at all. That requires more than routine customer onboarding and sanctions-list screening. Banks must scrutinize beneficial ownership and counterparties more closely and examine the purpose of payments, and anti-money-laundering teams must devote resources to reviewing transaction documentation and looking for payment patterns indicating that seemingly ordinary transactions may actually be moving money for sanctioned Iranian entities.

The US Treasury is now explicitly pushing this investigative burden onto foreign banks. In April, the Office of Foreign Assets Control urged financial institutions to subject independent teapot oil refineries in China to enhanced due diligence and warned that the US government is prepared to use secondary sanctions against them. The Treasury has since made clear that its latest sanctions campaign, Operation Economic Outcast, could include cutting foreign banks off from the dollar-based system.

In principle, Chinese law already requires banks to conduct “know your customer” verification and maintain financial-crime controls. In 2022, the Financial Action Task Force rated China’s anti-money-laundering regime as “largely compliant” with its due-diligence standards.

China has implemented additional measures since then. Its revised anti-money-laundering law, which took effect in January 2025, requires financial institutions to verify customers and beneficial owners, understand the nature of business relationships, and, in certain high-risk cases, investigate the source of funds and the purpose of transactions. Banks must also monitor customers and transactions and investigate activity that departs from established patterns. More detailed rules implemented in January 2026 allow banks to refuse transactions or terminate relationships when they cannot adequately resolve money-laundering concerns.

But anti-money-laundering compliance and US sanctions enforcement are not the same thing. Finding an Iranian connection may prompt a Chinese bank to look more closely at a transaction if there are signs of money laundering. It does not, however, mean that under Chinese law they must reject it just because the US has sanctioned one of the parties.

In some cases, Chinese regulations pull banks in the opposite direction. In May, the Chinese Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) issued a blocking order covering five independent Chinese refiners sanctioned by the US for purchasing Iranian oil. Four are smaller regional teapot refiners. The fifth, Hengli Petrochemical’s Dalian refinery, can process 400,000 barrels a day and belongs to the Hengli Group, a Fortune 500 company. It is the largest Chinese refiner sanctioned by the US so far.

MOFCOM’s order states that US sanctions against these five refiners “must not be recognized, implemented, or complied with.” Violations of the order can result in administrative penalties and expose banks and other companies to claims for damages in Chinese courts. A Chinese bank can still refuse to process a transaction because of money-laundering concerns or other compliance risks, but it cannot refuse a transaction or sever a relationship specifically to comply with the covered US sanctions without violating the order.

As the US extends secondary sanctions to cover more economically and politically significant Chinese entities, such blocking orders are likely to become more common. China now has a sophisticated legal and administrative apparatus that can make the extraterritorial application of US sanctions increasingly difficult — or, in some cases, moot.

This exposes a structural constraint on US sanctions power. Large state-owned Chinese banks have too much to lose if they are cut off from the dollar system. But US leverage weakens as transactions move to smaller banks with fewer ties to the US and Western financial markets.

The US government is thus left in the awkward position of asking Chinese banks to uncover hidden ties to sanctioned entities in Iran (or North Korea and Russia) and then act on those findings, even when that could put them at odds with Chinese law. Chinese banks are certainly willing to carry out the anti-money-laundering checks required by Chinese regulations, but they have little incentive to go looking for links to sanctioned entities when discovering them could create new legal problems.

In such circumstances, knowing less and maintaining plausible deniability is institutionally safer than knowing more. And unless Chinese banks closely police their own clients as payment networks adapt, sanctions will remain porous, with payments migrating to new shell companies and intermediaries.

Despite having the tools to retaliate against new US sanctions, China has used them selectively. Since US President Donald Trump restored “maximum pressure” on Iran in February 2025, US sanctions against Chinese entities have mostly targeted specific shadow-fleet vessels, independent refineries in Shandong Province, and shipping terminal operators (Hengli Petrochemical’s Dalian refinery, the only large integrated Chinese independent refiner sanctioned so far, remains the notable exception). China’s response has consisted mostly of formulaic Foreign Ministry statements rejecting the unilateral nature of US sanctions and pledging to protect Chinese companies and citizens.

MOFCOM’s May 2 blocking order remains the only consequential countermeasure, and it is narrow and targeted. Yet only days after it was issued, Chinese financial regulators reportedly instructed major Chinese banks to suspend new renminbi lending to the five sanctioned refiners while leaving existing credit lines in place.

These actions are not necessarily contradictory. China can reject the extraterritorial application of US sanctions while allowing major Chinese banks to protect themselves from the consequences. It has followed the same pattern since Operation Economic Outcast expanded secondary sanctions in August, criticizing the measures without imposing another Iran-related countermeasure.

The calculation could change if the US sanctioned a major Chinese bank or state-owned enterprise rather than another shell company, small bank, or teapot refiner. China’s largest financial institutions depend heavily on access to dollars. The US has far less leverage over smaller and less systemically important firms. This asymmetry makes an escalating spiral of US sanctions and Chinese countermeasures less likely.

The problem for the Trump administration is what happens as more transactions move beyond the institutions and payment channels most exposed to US pressure. At that point, effective enforcement increasingly requires cooperation from Chinese banks over which the US government has no authority.

A growing renminbi-based financial system does not make US sanctions ineffective, at least while major Chinese banks remain dependent on the global dollar-based system. But when non-dollar payments are routed through shadow intermediaries, they erode the two critical enforcement advantages on which US financial sanctions have traditionally relied: the visibility of transactions and leverage over the institutions that process them.

While the dollar system gives the US enormous financial power, American officials can no longer assume that the threat of being excluded from it will be enough to make foreign institutions comply with their dictates. As more of the actual enforcement takes place inside China’s domestic financial system, beyond the reach of American authorities, China may gain a new source of geopolitical leverage.

Expecting China to enforce US sanctions is unrealistic, but anti-money-laundering enforcement offers a more practical basis for cooperation. As US and Chinese officials discuss Iran and its financial ties to China ahead of Trump’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, the US would have better luck pressing China to enforce its own anti-money-laundering rules against the opaque financial networks facilitating Iranian trade.

The writer is Senior Fellow for China Studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, is Adjunct Professor of International and Public Affairs at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs. Copyright: Project Syndicate, 2026.
