editorials.title: From fibre to future: Weaving sustainability into India's textile growth
editorials.passage:
As India targets a $350 billion textile and apparel industry by 2030, sustainability is shifting from the margins to the centre of its competitiveness strategy. For a sector spanning fibre, yarn, fabric, processing, apparel, technical textiles and made-ups, sustainability is increasingly becoming a question of competitiveness, market access and responsible growth.

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi said, “The world is adopting the vision of Fashion for Environment and Empowerment, and India can lead the way in this regard,” he pointed to a transformation that is increasingly visible across India’s textile landscape.

The textile sector is a major employment engine, directly supporting over 49 million livelihoods. Its domestic market is valued at about $196 billion and is projected to reach $250 billion by 2030, while India is targeting $100 billion in textile exports by the same year.

The Ministry of Textiles’ sustainability agenda reflects this dual reality. It is built around a simple proposition: India should not have to choose between growth and sustainability. Instead, cleaner production, resource efficiency, circularity and responsible manufacturing are set to become the foundation of the textile sector’s next growth chapter.

Global brands are setting increasingly ambitious sustainability targets for their supply chains. Consumers are showing greater interest in reused, repaired and recycled products, while policymakers in major export markets are introducing requirements related to environmental performance, recycled content, traceability, chemicals, water and energy use. India’s climate commitments — including 500 GW of non-fossil energy capacity, 50 per cent of energy requirements from renewables and net zero emissions by 2070 — are also steering the textile sector towards a low-carbon growth trajectory. For Indian exporters, sustainability is therefore moving beyond a peripheral compliance issue and becoming an integral part of industrial competitiveness.

India also starts from a position of strength, with a large manufacturing base, diverse raw materials, technical capabilities, an established recycling and reuse ecosystem, a growing start-up landscape and a wide network of clusters, research institutions and industry associations. Circularity is not entirely new to India. Traditions such as rafugari, kantha, godhadis, chindi durries and khesh weaving have embedded repair, reuse and repurposing in communities for generations. India’s hosting of the World Circular Economy Forum 2026 further reflects this larger shift, bringing together governments, industry, innovators and experts together to turn ideas into partnerships and scalable solutions.

One of the clearest areas to put circularity into practice is textile waste. A Ministry study from 2026, covering 15 states and more than 250 stakeholder interactions, estimated annual textile waste generation at 70.73 lakh tonnes. More than 70 per cent is already recovered and routed into recycling, downcycling or upcycling streams, with recovery of pre-consumer waste exceeding 95 per cent. The larger gap is post-consumer waste, where collection, segregation and economically viable recovery systems remain less developed. The study estimated that India’s textile recycling market could reach about $3.5 billion by 2030, with opportunities across collection, sorting, fibre recovery, recycling, upcycling, repair and sustainable manufacturing, with the potential to generate around one lakh green jobs.

The Ministry is moving beyond quantifying the problem to building the infrastructure and market mechanisms needed to close the loop. Textile recovery facilities are being piloted in multiple cities, while textile-waste mapping is identifying the need for stronger collection and sorting systems and policy solutions for blended and non-recyclable materials. A textile-waste management pilot in Navi Mumbai, implemented by the Textiles Committee in partnership with Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation, Saahas Foundation and women’s self-help groups, diverted more than 3,323 kg of textile waste from landfill and incineration, reached over 12,000 families and installed more than 80 collection bins. It also produced over 1,000 samples and upcycled products. Through a partnership between the Textiles Committee, Government e-Marketplace (GeM) and SCOPE, certified upcycled textile products are being brought into public procurement. 31 upcyclers have been certified under the upcycled textile mark, with 27 categories and 40 products live on GeM, helping create an assured market for circular products.

Circularity is only one part of the sustainability story. Much of the environmental footprint of textiles is created during manufacturing and processing, making water, energy and chemicals equally important. The agenda of eliminating hazardous chemicals is being taken up through a major programme with UNIDO, the Global Environment Facility and other partners.

The project aims to reduce hazardous chemicals while improving energy, water and greenhouse gas performance. Its targets include reducing 10,530 tonnes of toxic chemicals directly and 21,000 tonnes indirectly, while mitigating 147,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent directly and 294,000 tonnes indirectly. It is also designed to directly reach 40,000 people, 60 per cent of whom are expected to be women. At the infrastructure level, sustainability is being built into the sector’s future industrial geography. Seven PM MITRA parks, with an expected investment of about $10 billion, are envisaged with integrated water, wastewater and common processing infrastructure.

For sustainability to become mainstream, pilots must move into factories and clusters. This is particularly important because a large part of the textile ecosystem comprises MSMEs, which may face constraints in accessing technology, finance, data and technical expertise. The Ministry constituted an ESG Task Force in July 2023, bringing together government bodies, industry associations, chambers, multilateral agencies, innovators, brands and academia. Its work focuses on harmonised certification, cluster handholding, awareness and capacity building, sustainable fashion technology, and the use of artificial intelligence and digitalisation for data and traceability. The ESG Task Force has supported the EU-India Resource Efficiency & Circular Economy Initiative (EU-I RECEI), implemented through GIZ, covering a national assessment of textile waste, a circular economy roadmap for Tamil Nadu, an MSME toolkit for Panipat and a standard operating procedure for Textile Recovery Facilities. A separate UNEP-led programme is providing life-cycle assessment and eco-innovation training and technical assistance to SMEs in the Surat and Karur clusters.

Technology and innovation are also long-term enablers. The National Technical Textiles Mission supports research into waste-to-fibre technologies and conversion of textile waste and bio-residues into advanced green materials. At IIT Delhi’s Panipat campus, the Atal Centre of Textile Recycling and Sustainability is undertaking research and technology transfer, including recycling heat-resistant aramid fibre waste used in defence and aerospace applications. At Bharat Tex 2026, sustainability-focused research on traceable hemp fibre, circular business models and wheat straw as a forest-free alternative for man-made cellulosic fibres further highlighted the breadth of innovation emerging around the sector.

The Union Budget 2026–27 provided a strong policy signal. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced an integrated programme for the labour-intensive textile sector, with Tex-Eco placing sustainability alongside fibre security, manufacturing expansion, traditional clusters, handlooms, handicrafts and skilling—not as a separate environmental programme, but as part of the sector’s growth architecture. The proposed Tex-Eco Initiative brings together four strategic pillars: resource recovery and recycling infrastructure; water stewardship and decarbonisation; institutionalising sustainability and building capability; and innovation, digital enablement and knowledge systems. Textile recycling mega-hubs and textile recovery facilities would support collection, sorting, grading and routing of textile waste. Water and decarbonisation measures would support ZLD, renewable energy, low-emission boilers and resource-efficient technologies. An India sustainability mark is proposed to strengthen market credibility, alongside assurance, compliance, capacity building and demand generation.

Behind these interventions is a broader institutional shift. A dedicated sustainability section within the Ministry of Textiles acts as a focal point for sustainable and circular practices, resource efficiency, environmental impact reduction, green technologies and responsible production. The government is positioned not only as a regulator but also as a facilitator, leader and implementing partner. The ESG agenda also goes beyond the environmental dimension. Worker welfare, formalisation, green jobs and a just transition sit alongside decarbonisation, water stewardship, chemical safety and circularity, while governance priorities include standards, traceability, disclosure, certification and assurance.

India’s textile sustainability journey is entering a critical phase, with the focus now on stronger post-consumer collection, recycling infrastructure, resource-efficient manufacturing, commercialisation of green technologies, credible measurement and traceability, and stronger markets for recycled and upcycled products. A proposed sustainability alliance would bring together government, UN agencies, financial institutions, industry, MSMEs and academia around these priorities. The direction is increasingly clear: sustainability must work for a factory owner as much as for the environment, for an exporter as much as for the consumer and for a large integrated park as much as for a small enterprise. This can improve resource productivity, unlock access to demanding global markets, spur new businesses around recycling and green technologies and generate employment.

For a nation on track to nearly double its textile and apparel market by 2030, sustainability is not about slowing growth. It is about powering the next wave of growth—cleaner, more circular, more resilient and ultimately more competitive.

(The writer is the Union Minister of Textiles. The views expressed are personal)

Published on September 18, 2026

editorials.title: Government health schemes at a crossroads
editorials.passage:
For more than seven decades, the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) has provided healthcare security to serving and retired government employees and their families. Long before health insurance became a mainstream policy objective in India, CGHS established an important principle: illness should not expose families to financial hardship and people should have access to quality healthcare when they need it.

That principle remains as relevant today as it was in 1954. But the system built around it needs to change.

The issue goes well beyond CGHS. The Railways, the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme (ECHS), the Central Armed Police Forces and several State governments operate their own health schemes for employees and pensioners. Their institutional arrangements differ, but many face a common challenge: inadequate budget provision, increasing pool of beneficiaries, rising healthcare costs, fragmented purchasing arrangements and inadequate incentives for either providers or beneficiaries to use resources efficiently.

As healthcare costs continue to rise at double-digit rates, this model cannot remain fiscally sustainable indefinitely.

The government’s recent revision of CGHS reimbursement rates was timely and necessary. Hospitals cannot be expected to provide quality care at rates that bear little relationship to the cost of delivering it. But periodically increasing reimbursement rates without reforming the underlying purchasing system risks treating the symptom rather than the disease.

The more fundamental question is not simply how much government pays for healthcare, but how it pays for it. This is where reform must begin.

First, government schemes need to move decisively away from fee-for-service payment. Under fee-for-service, every additional consultation, investigation or procedure generates additional revenue for the provider. The incentives therefore favour more services rather than better outcomes or greater efficiency.

Wherever feasible, payment should instead be based on well-defined treatment packages. A hospital treating a patient for a particular condition should receive a predetermined amount covering the entire episode of care, rather than billing separately for every investigation, procedure and consumable. Over time, India should move towards more sophisticated systems such as diagnosis-related groups, which adjust payments for the complexity of patients while encouraging efficient treatment. Better-designed packages would reduce both administrative complexity and opportunities for over-treatment.

Second, medicines offer another major opportunity for efficiency. Government should use its enormous purchasing power far more effectively. Generic medicines of assured quality should be the default across government schemes, supported by strong formularies, bulk procurement, better inventory management and prescription audits.

The potential savings are substantial. Medicine expenditure is one of the fastest-growing components of CGHS expenditure, with excessive dependence on purchases through authorised local chemists rather than more efficient procurement channels. The objective should not be to restrict access to medicines but to obtain the same quality at a substantially lower cost.

Third, gatekeeping needs to become much more effective. A health system in which patients can move directly to expensive specialist and tertiary care without appropriate clinical referral will inevitably become costly.

CGHS already has an important asset in its network of wellness centres. These should become genuine coordinators of care — providing strong primary care, managing chronic diseases, ensuring preventive screening and referring patients to specialists when clinically necessary. Similar mechanisms should be strengthened in ECHS, Railways and state employee schemes. Effective gatekeeping is not about denying care. It is about ensuring that the patient receives the right care, at the right level, at the right time.

Fourth, we need a mature discussion about beneficiary contributions. When healthcare is completely free at the point of use, with virtually unlimited benefits, some degree of moral hazard is inevitable. This does not justify imposing substantial financial burdens on pensioners or people with serious illnesses. But modest and carefully designed co-payments or deductibles for selected services, particularly treatment in private hospitals, deserve consideration.

Such provisions can be differentiated by income, age and type of service, with appropriate exemptions for vulnerable groups and chronic conditions. Even a small element of cost sharing can influence utilisation behaviour without undermining financial protection.

There is also a larger structural question. Why should different arms of government separately empanel hospitals, negotiate prices, process claims, build IT systems and establish anti-fraud mechanisms for essentially similar populations?

Greater convergence across CGHS, ECHS, ESI, Railways and other government schemes could create larger risk pools and vastly strengthen the government’s purchasing power. This effort should be led by the National Health Authority that implements my most cherished scheme Ayushman Bharat. Complete institutional merger may take time and may not always be feasible, but common provider networks, standard treatment packages, shared technology platforms, interoperable claims systems and coordinated price negotiations should be entirely achievable. State governments could increasingly adopt the same architecture.

None of this diminishes the importance of fixing the operational problems that providers rightly highlight today. Payments must be timely. Hospitals need visibility into the claims lifecycle. Grievances and disputes must be resolved within clearly defined timelines. Digital platforms should simplify rather than complicate transactions. Fraud controls must be strong but should not become an excuse for delaying legitimate payments.

Public health programmes ultimately depend on partnerships. Governments finance healthcare, providers deliver healthcare and patients benefit from healthcare. When providers have confidence in the system, they are more willing to invest, innovate and expand capacity. When confidence weakens, the impact is eventually felt by beneficiaries.

CGHS has been one of India’s most enduring healthcare success stories.

The opportunity before policymakers today is not to dismantle what has worked but to strengthen its foundations for the future — and to apply these lessons across government health schemes.

The recent revision in CGHS rates was an important first step. The next step must be more ambitious: moving from simply paying healthcare bills to strategically purchasing healthcare. That is the transition required to ensure that the schemes relied upon by millions remain affordable, efficient, transparent and trusted by those who sustain them every day.

The writer, a Senior Associate with Johns Hopkins University, was founding CEO of Ayushman Bharat

editorials.title: More crop output, but for farmers the gains are less
editorials.passage:
India’s agricultural journey is one of the country’s great development successes. Foodgrain production increased from 51 million tonnes in 1950-51 to nearly 358 million tonnes in 2024-25. The country now feeds more than a billion people, and exports agricultural commodities to global markets. It is another matter that production could come under stress this kharif owing to El Nino, with 43 per cent of the country facing a rain deficit amid indications of an acreage drop.

Nevertheless, it can be said that output has not posed serious concerns over time. This achievement was built through the efforts of farmers, scientists, policymakers, extension workers, cooperatives and public institutions. The Green Revolution transformed Indian agriculture and helped secure the nation’s future.

But if agricultural progress is primarily measured by production, why does farmers’ prosperity remain elusive? Why have direct benefit transfers, such as PM-KISAN and State-level income support schemes, become enduring features of agricultural policy? And why do national surveys continue to indicate that a significant proportion of farmers would prefer to leave agriculture?

The changing composition of farm household income tells its own story. According to the NSS (SAS-77 round), crop cultivation contributes about 37 per cent of household income, while wages account for 40 per cent, with livestock and non-farm activities making up the balance. Rural households increasingly had to diversify their income sources in response to changing economic realities and growing risks.

Yet, the contrast is striking. Foodgrain production has increased nearly seven-fold since Independence, but these gains have not translated into commensurate improvements in farm household incomes.

The challenge before Indian agriculture today is very different from that of the 1960s. Then, the overriding concern was food security. Today, the agenda is broader and more complex: soil health, groundwater depletion, climate resilience, market volatility, nutritional security, farm incomes and the ability of farming to attract the next generation.

Taken together, these trends suggest the need for a fresh assessment of Indian agriculture — not merely its production performance — but also the institutions, policies and innovation systems that support it.

India possesses one of the world’s largest public agricultural research systems. ICAR and the State Agricultural Universities have generated a vast body of scientific knowledge and released thousands of crop varieties over the decades. Yet, the more important question is: how many of these varieties continue to find widespread acceptance among farmers? How many also remain relevant under increasingly uncertain climatic conditions?

How many of these varieties are cultivated on a significant scale? Which varieties account for the bulk of cultivated area in major crops? Which continue to be preferred by farmers and why? And how many have demonstrated resilience not merely in research stations, but in farmers’ fields exposed to increasingly erratic weather? After all, a variety released is an output; a variety adopted and sustained by farmers is an outcome. The distinction matters.

These questions are not merely academic. They help us understand where innovation is succeeding, who is driving it, and how its impact should be assessed.

In hybrid vegetable crops, private innovation has achieved notable farmer acceptance. India is one of the world’s largest vegetable producers and imports substantial quantities of vegetable seeds.

This raises important questions about how well our broader innovation system is responding to farmers’ evolving needs and preferences. This is not about public versus private. Rather, it is an opportunity for the public system — with its vast resources — to reflect on what farmers value, and ensure that its innovations remain relevant, resilient and widely adopted.

Farmers adopt varieties that satisfy a complex combination of yield, risk, consumer preference, market acceptance, shelf life and profitability. As the challenges facing agriculture evolve, our institutions, policies and innovation systems must evolve with them. The more relevant questions today are whether they are responding to farmers’ changing needs, anticipating emerging risks and strengthening resilience. Are we adequately preparing agriculture for droughts, floods, heat stress and erratic weather? Are we helping farmers remain productive, profitable and adaptable in a far more uncertain environment?

These questions acquire added significance in an era of climate uncertainty. Agriculture today must contend with droughts, extreme rainfall, rising temperatures, volatile markets and other emerging risks. Production and productivity will remain important, but they may no longer be sufficient measures of success.

It may, therefore, be time to develop composite metrics for the institutions and agencies that shape and support agriculture. Such metrics could track farm incomes, farmer retention, adoption of new technologies, soil health, groundwater sustainability, resilience under climatic stress and the long-term performance of innovations in farmers’ fields. What gets measured often influences what gets prioritised.

The writer is the former Deputy Managing Director of Nabard. Views are personal

Published on September 18, 2026

editorials.title: Should GST be imposed on MDR?
editorials.passage:
“Since currently no MDR is charged on UPI transactions, there is consequently no GST .” With these words, the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) put to rest, in April 2025, rumours that UPI payments above ₹2,000 would be taxed. From 15 October 2026, merchants will pay a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.4 per cent on person-to-merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300, with a flat ₹5 for categories such as railways, telecom, fuel and insurance. Where there is MDR, there is GST at 18 per cent. The law plainly permits the levy. The question is whether it should be imposed.

The MDR is consideration for processing and settling a payment — a supply of service under Section 7 of the CGST Act, 2017, classified among financial and related services and taxed at 18 per cent. GST is not levied for the ₹50,000 paid for a refrigerator; it touches only the ₹200 fee, adding ₹36. At the cap, the merchant pays ₹300 plus ₹54.

During the zero-MDR years since January 2020, banks were compensated through a budgetary incentive scheme. On the GST Council’s recommendation, CBIC clarified in Circular No. 190/02/2023-GST that these incentives are subsidies directly linked to price, excluded from the value of supply under Section 15.

Two justifications may be offered for the levy: neutrality, since a service is a service, and revenue, which practitioners estimate at ₹3,500 crore to over ₹5,000 crore a year.

The revenue figure is largely illusory. A registered supplier making taxable supplies will claim input tax credit, so the transaction is tax neutral. Net revenue comes only from those who cannot claim credit: the unregistered trader whose UPI receipts exceed ₹1 lakh a month but whose turnover is below the registration threshold, the composition dealer barred by Section 10 from availing credit, and those making exempt supplies. The real burden thus falls on the small and the exempt — the merchants the ₹2,000 threshold was meant to protect. For them, GST becomes a cost embedded in price, the cascading GST was designed to end, and the effective charge rises to 0.472 per cent. That is a nudge back towards cash in trades with single-digit margins. Retailers have already warned that the MDR alone could reverse hard won digital adoption as the festive season approaches; GST sharpens that risk.

Neutrality is equally unpersuasive, because GST law is not neutral here. Notification No. 12/2017–Central Tax (Rate) already exempts services by an acquiring bank for settlement of amounts up to ₹2,000 per transaction through payment cards. Relief for small-value digital settlement is already part of the architecture – this should be extended for consistency.

When the government paid banks for processing UPI payments, the payment was a non-taxable subsidy. When the merchant pays for the same service, 18 per cent GST applies- this contradiction must be resolved.

The State has also designed the MDR itself. It prescribes and caps the rate, forbids its recovery from consumers, and earmarks 5 per cent of collections for expanding acceptance among small merchants. In substance, it is a regulated contribution to the upkeep of public digital infrastructure, for which the Budget provides ₹2,000 crore in FY 2026-27 against industry estimates of about ₹20,000 crore in annual running costs. To tax a charge that exists because budgetary support fell short is to take back with one hand what the government asks merchants to give with the other.

Under the European Union’s VAT Directive, Article 135(1)(d) exempts transactions concerning payments and transfers, and many VAT jurisdictions treat core financial services as exempt. Exemption has costs — banks would reverse proportionate input tax credit — but the comparison shows that taxing payment infrastructure is a policy choice, not a legal inevitability.

At their October meeting, the GST Council should extend the existing card-settlement exemption to MDR on UPI merchant payments or, if revenue is a concern, prescribe a concessional rate of 5 per cent. Net of input tax credit, the revenue foregone is small; the signal to millions of small merchants is large. UPI is India’s most celebrated public digital good. The government kept the cost of sustaining UPI outside the GST net when it paid that cost itself. The same logic must hold when merchants bear it.

The writer is a chartered accountant

Published on September 18, 2026

editorials.title: NEET debate is still wide open
editorials.passage: The cancellation of NEET this year, following allegations of paper leak, had become the focal point around which the youth gathered in thousands to protest at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar in June July this year. The protests are over, but they have reignited past discussions around the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET), and how it should be conducted. So far, two strong but competing arguments have kept policy makers, politicians and academics engaged: i) should not states, which also legislate on education, be allowed to conduct exams for admission to medical colleges set up by them and those by the private sector in their region? and, ii) should not there be a basic minimum national standard for admitting students into medical colleges, whichever state they might be in? Conversations with officers in states and the Centre over the last two months bring to fore certain new aspects. ALSO READPoor in economic security Number 1: A top police officer of a big city digressed from a discussion on how the Delhi police could have done better to avoid the terrible showdown with the youth at Jantar Mantar on July 20. “Had it not been for NEET… if only states were the owners of the medical exams and admissions… the protests would not have happened in the national capital,” he said. Given a choice, his cadre state, ruled by the BJP, would be only too keen to reclaim ownership of medical entrance exams, the officer said. But then the Centre, also under the BJP, had, in its wisdom, fought a long legal battle going up to the Supreme Court, to implement NEET. No BJP Chief Minister of a state will now risk going against this. The officer did not say it in as many  words, but he linked law and order to NEET ownership. Isn’t the Centre better off with states taking charge of the exam? The unitary character of the exam had indeed directed student anger towards Delhi and the  Union Ministry of Education. It forced Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to step down. Number 2: It’s not just about law and order; it is also about the administration of a country-wide exam. Consider the numbers for the May 3 NEET exam: 22 lakh students, 5,432 centres, 551 cities. Conducting such an exam at the same time on the same day in a country of this size involves phenomenal planning and logistics. From the integrity of paper-setters to safe and secure transportation of question papers, the challenges are numerous. None is insurmountable, though. For instance, when the NEET re-exam was to be conducted on June 21 with just six weeks of lead time, the government did not mind pressing into service the Indian Air Force for delivering question papers in the nick of time at different locations. But the problem is not of scale. It is the inability to insulate a local problem. An officer in the Centre, who was roped in to ensure an orderly conduct of the June 21 retest, likened NEET to a super-tanker. A small chink can bring down the entire supertanker. A leak of a paper in a particular city or an irregularity in a few centres can potentially wreck the entire examination. ALSO READBoard audits: Myth, miracle, or mirage When there are already so many reasons for the youth to be disoriented, an exam cancellation can trigger a nationwide movement, as it did recently. Number 3: Another officer pointed to the blindspots many in the system carry with them. More than a decade ago, just after the BJP came to power in the Centre, a meeting was called to discuss NEET. When Tamil Nadu, one of the most vocal opponents of NEET, put forth its views, an officer in the Ministry of Education, who was from north India, said many exams are cancelled in his state and NEET would set this right. To this, the Tamil Nadu officer recalled his one-sentence reply: “This might be the case in your state, not in mine.” There are reasons why the Centre did what it did, and these will always be open to question and debate in India’s federal polity. Memory is short, but the idea of a common all-India examination as a qualifier for admissions to all medical colleges, first found mention in December 2010. The change proposed by the Medical Council of India (now the National Medical Commission) was intended to ease the academic pressure on students. The first NEET examination was held by the CBSE in 2013 when the Congress-led UPA was in power. The BJP carried forward this agenda with full vigour and seriousness despite strident opposition from states such as Tamil Nadu. The writer is Managing Editor, The Indian Express. Off the Record is a fortnightly column

editorials.title: Inside Track by Coomi Kapoor: Uncurated visuals go viral
editorials.passage: Uncurated visuals go viral BRICS summit 2026 was perhaps the first major international conference in Delhi where the Ministry of External Affairs cut the Information and Broadcasting Ministry out of the loop. Normally at such events, the I&B department handles duties such as liaising with domestic and international media, preparing background material and briefs, local facilitation for visitors and covering up embarrassing moments. Without the seasoned hand of the I&B to smooth wrinkles, some of the unedited optics at the conference went viral.  The decision to transport all central ministers and chief ministers from Parliament House to the Bharat Mandapam in two buses may have been taken elsewhere — but senior leaders such as Amit Shah, J P Nadda and Yogi Adityanath are unlikely to have been amused with reels showing them huddled together in a bus! Only Prime Minister Modi had a separate cavalcade to reach the Mandapam, along with most of the foreign heads of state. ALSO READPoor in economic security Some felt the bus journey was unnecessary. Considering the sealed corridor from Parliament House to the Mandapam was, in any case, fairly empty and fully secure, a few extra ministerial cars on this route would have made little difference.  Another awkward video widely shared, possibly exaggerated by AI, was of National Security Advisor Ajit Doval munching cashews sitting to the rear of Russian President Vladimir Putin and the MEA’s official spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal nibbling nuts continuously, though seated right behind Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in the full glare of the TV cameras. Finally, the MEA’s reel of a young woman extolling every minor item presented in the goodies gift bag to journalists, from toothbrush to notebook, was cringe-worthy. The publicity should have focused on the gains of the Delhi declaration, not memes, on the misguided notion they would attract young viewership. Diplomatic concessions Since 2012, the MEA has followed a policy of disallowing meetings between visiting foreign heads and opposition political leaders or activists, under the radar of security agencies. But for BRICS, the government understood that to further its foreign relations’ objectives, exceptions had to be made. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim was permitted to breakfast with Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Vadra, and he tweeted their interaction, describing Rahul as a good friend who briefed him on current affairs and foreign issues. ALSO READBoard audits: Myth, miracle, or mirage Ibrahim is grateful to the Congress because when he was in jail in his homeland, then-PM Manmohan Singh offered to facilitate the education of his sons abroad. An exception was also made for Ibrahim, a devout Muslim, to call on Islamic clerics in Kerala. Meanwhile, at the request of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, controversial Hurriyat Conference leader Mirwaiz Farooq, who has frequently been detained in Kashmir, was permitted to attend a diplomatic reception in Delhi hosted by the Iranian embassy for its president. Later, Mirwaiz had a long conversation with Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi. Keeping media guessing Ever since BJP President Nitin Nabin announced his team, the media and people who claim to be in the know — if that is indeed possible in this closed-door regime — have speculated that a ministerial reshuffle is in the offing. However, with the inauspicious ‘Pitru Paksha’ period set to begin shortly, followed by Dussehra and Diwali, ministerial changes may take a while yet. But three gubernatorial announcements, including a new LG for Jammu and Kashmir, could be announced earlier. Only blind loyalists wanted Rahul Gandhi’s deep distrust of anyone perceived as a defector or party rebel is a drawback in helping Congress increase its footprint. The latest setback for the party is in Goa, where assembly elections are due early next year. The Congress missed a golden opportunity to re-admit the popular Goa Forward Party leader, Vijai Sardesai, who has represented the Fatorda assembly constituency in South Goa since 2012. Party President Mallikarjun Kharge met Sardesai in May and has been waiting for a word from Rahul to permit him. But without any welcoming word, Sardesai decided to accept Arvind Kejriwal’s offer to join AAP, a move which would divide the Opposition vote. Political party, not bureaucracy The BJP government appears nervous and on the back foot, but Rahul Gandhi, as Leader of Opposition, has not been able to seize the moment to the extent expected. He, instead of touring and building public opinion, has been bogged down in a time-consuming exercise, selecting junior level party office-bearers. The procedure is unnecessarily bureaucratic, with candidates shortlisted after  getting recommendation letters from state party in-charges or central office-bearers. The stamp of General Secretary (Organisation) KC Venugopal in most selections is obvious.

editorials.title: Don’t discount Reform because it’s had a bad year. In our angry, fragile democracy, anything can happen
editorials.passage:
D espite the energised start Andy Burnham has made as prime minister, plenty of his party’s MPs and hardcore activists are still haunted by a familiar sense of insecurity. Underpinned by a political version of impostor syndrome, it runs deep – and, bar the odd spell of Labour optimism, it always has. So it is with the battle between Labour and Reform UK that will define an election that could arrive much sooner than some people think, and a widely held ambivalence on the left about the possibility of Nigel Farage’s party taking power. Reform is apparently in deep trouble, yet also still in with a serious chance. How come?

Investigations into the party and its leadership’s finances by both the Metropolitan police and parliament’s standards commissioner may worsen Reform’s woes. Those investigations predate the two recently announced £36m donations from the crypto tycoons Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, which themselves risk being backdatedly ruled illegal and are reportedly already being spent on 400 “field agents”. The two mega-donations symbolise two connected stories. One is about the possible buyout of our fragile democracy. The other centres on how, from much of the public’s perspective, all the allegations about Farage and his party might have already turned into an indecipherable blizzard. So, although Reform is down, it is still far from out.

But the reasons for that extend much further than money. Reform still has a serious chance of either leading or forming the next government because of the same basic fact that Burnham says he has come to avenge: that since the crash of 2008, millions of British lives have pinballed from one crisis to the next, leaving many people resentful, insecure and plain scared.

If anyone hadn’t already noticed, ours is an age of fear: of economic insecurity, wildfires and unprecedented weather, seemingly unending wars, and massed and chaotic human movement. Reform – and the Tories – lean into all that anxiety, offering the kind of crass solutions (witness Farage’s recent promise of a state of “ national emergency ” as soon as he takes office) that only heighten people’s sense of crisis. Labour, meanwhile, can only offer another variation of its age-old answer: modest hope and constructive change. Such will be the choice sooner or later presented to voters. And in that sense, the next election will be more emotional than political.

Make no mistake: the campaign has effectively already begun. If, for instance, John Healey’s first budget is not peppered with vivid symbols of a different approach to the economy, it will threaten to be a very serious dud, with lasting consequences. Moreover, at some point during the autumn – presumably beginning at the Labour conference – we will start to get a sense of Burnham’s 10-year plan. He will have to talk about AI, and its dire threats and huge opportunities, and the climate emergency – a subject he has so far been strangely reluctant to address . But he will also need convincing answers to less apocalyptic problems. Right now, I can think of no better example than the million or so young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) who have mums, dads and grandparents terrified – fear, once again – on their behalf.

He is also going to have to walk some very precarious tightropes. We all know what sits behind much of the public’s feelings about immigration: as well as misapprehensions about the relevant numbers – which are actually going down – and straight-up racism, too many working lives sit on the borderline between the official and illicit economy, and are defined by “employers being able to import cheap agency labour to undercut existing pay and conditions in the name of free-market orthodoxy”. Those last words were once uttered by that sainted socialist Jeremy Corbyn: they were intended as a rational explanation for yet another example of people’s deep sense of worry.

From that vantage point, footage of so-called small boats is bound often to spark a callous and fearful response. To many people, such sights look – look – like proof of even more people who have come to disappear into the cracks that run through our labour market, and then surface offering to work longer hours than you, for a lot less money. That makes you feel even more scared than you already were. And as any student of the 20th century knows, nothing warps politics – and helps demagogues – like that kind of anxiety.

A visceral dread is now the basis of the picture of modern Britain – and England in particular – offered to the public by Reform, the Tories and their allies in the press and online. We are, in fact, living through the comprehensive reinvention of English rightwing politics as a byword for angst, fury and paranoia. Anything that could reasonably be termed conservatism is nowhere to be seen: their England is now a country where summers are spent willing on unrest , and where quasi-paramilitaries menace our ports . Last week saw that Passport to Pimlico-esque village of Piddington in Oxfordshire hold a referendum on leaving the UK – with 92% of votes in favour – because of what the Telegraph calls a “migrant camp”. From Reform in particular, one often gets the sense that any degree of contentment is seen as being tantamount to complacent wokeness; as they see it, England is – or should be – a righteously stroppy little country, prone to the raging, nihilistic impulses that Farage et al seem to see as the essence of our national character.

As much as Labour needs a solid, credible approach to immigration, it is going to have to remind people of the truth. We are a country with problems, for sure, but one whose people have not abandoned hope and largely get along with one other – and where, to quote July’s bulletin from the Office for National Statistics, “The cost of living (88%), the NHS (78%) and the economy (70%) were the most commonly reported issues facing the UK today.” Whatever our fears, earlier this month, YouGov reported that 57% of us are “fairly satisfied” with life. Labour should attack Farage, Badenoch et al for their lack of faith in the essential moderation and calm of most Britons; Burnham is the first senior Labour figure in a long time who may have the authenticity, energy and principle to make such talk actually ring true.

And then there are more solid, tangible matters. A fortnight ago, the new prime minister announced £1bn of investment in a new fleet of trains that are going to be built in Derby, “supporting over 350 jobs … and almost 6,000 across [the] UK supply chain”. Self-evidently, we need a lot more of that kind of stuff. Highly visible sites should be quickly set aside for new council housing, so Labour can point at the plots and promise people transformed and secure lives. In our further education colleges, money must soon be spent on teaching the absent skills that will help revive the economy, not least in construction, and provide good, dependable jobs.

The list inevitably goes on, but it may soon mark the difference between the meaningful survival of our democracy and the arrival of a munificently funded barbarism. Labour high-ups ought to remind themselves that that great Labour godhead Aneurin Bevan titled his only book In Place of Fear : in those four words lie this new government’s basic mission, the high stakes involved, and the almost impossibly hard work it will take to even begin to achieve it.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: From Lizzie Borden to Myra Hindley, why are we still so fascinated with female killers?
editorials.passage:
O n 20 June 1893, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, a packed courtroom waited with bated breath for the jury to return its verdict following a gruelling double-murder trial. Against a backdrop of intense media interest, they had heard the prosecution argue that the accused had hacked to death their own parents with a hatchet, had burned their clothing to hide evidence of blood, and had done so out of hatred. The question the jury was asked to answer was simple – was Lizzie Andrew Borden guilty of murdering her father and stepmother? Jurors took just one hour to reach a decision: not guilty.

Yet, almost as soon as the trial came to an end, the mythmaking around Borden began – from fevered speculation about her motives and the infamous nursery rhyme to the many film and TV retellings of the story. The latest incarnation, Netflix’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story , opens with an axe-wielding Borden committing the murders, and frames the crimes around a fictionalised queer romance between her and the family’s housemaid, Bridget Sullivan.

Why, after 130 years, are we still enthralled by the Borden murders? Part of the answer, I think, speaks to a wider obsession with female killers (or alleged female killers in Borden’s case) and the way in which society ties itself in knots to try to explain, excuse or justify violent women. Statistically, globally and historically, homicide is a largely male crime – in terms of both perpetrators and victims. Female killers are rare: they represented just 7% of convicted homicide suspects in England and Wales between 2019 and 2022. It is precisely this rarity that sees homicides with female perpetrators (or alleged perpetrators) disproportionately sensationalised, mythologised and forced into recognisable tropes – the femme fatale, the wrongfully accused, the passive victim or the monstrosity.

That is not to say there isn’t some truth in each of these ideas . But very often a female perpetrator of a violent crime will also trigger or become the face of wider societal debates about crime, punishment, justice and womanhood. History is littered with examples.

The execution of Marie Manning in 1849, alongside her husband, for the murder of her lover, Patrick O’Connor, was followed by tens of thousands of Londoners, including Charles Dickens , and spawned close to 2.5m broadsheet sales. The shock of seeing a woman hanged triggered a nationwide debate about the ethics of public executions (they were abolished in Britain less than 20 years later). So notorious did Manning become that Madame Tussauds created a wax model of her, dressed in the black satin dress the killer supposedly wore at her execution . The statue remained in its chamber of horrors until 1971.

Similarly, the trial of the chocolate poisoner, Christiana Edmunds, forced Victorian society to confront the idea that a single middle-class woman could intentionally cause indiscriminate harm. When an attempted plea of insanity failed and she was found guilty of the murder of Sidney Barker and attempted murder of Mrs Beard, she was sentenced to death. But the home secretary stepped in, asked for her to be reassessed and granted her a reprieve. She spent the rest of her days at Broadmoor psychiatric hospital.

As the historian Jill Newton Ainsley attests , “Declaring her insane and therefore not responsible for her actions provided a bizarre and unprecedented crime with a relatively simple explanation.” This reluctance to acknowledge women’s agency when it comes to violent crime plays out in statistics too. Newton Ainsley has shown that between 1832 and 1901 women were twice as likely as men to be granted an acquittal on the grounds of insanity – even when charged with similar crimes.

For very different reasons, the acquittal of Beatrice Pace in 1928 captured public attention. She had been accused of murdering her abusive husband by arsenic poisoning, only to become the poster girl for wronged women. Upon her acquittal, newspapers reported emotional scenes where “women clasped one another by the hands and some cried”. Hundreds of women later wrote to her expressing their well wishes for her future. A few decades later, in 1955, after shooting her abusive lover, David Blakely, five times with a revolver, there was no such sympathy for Ruth Ellis at her trial. She was found guilty of murder, but her subsequent execution shone a spotlight on the ethics of capital punishment .

Perhaps the most chilling manifestation of female violence in the 20th century comes in the person of the child killer Myra Hindley. Despite conducting the crimes alongside Ian Brady, the criminologist Mark Pettigrew has noted that the press coverage of Hindley, with the infamous mugshot, far exceeded that of Brady. Additionally, her unsuccessful parole attempts opened a wider debate about whether “life” should mean life. More recently, the case of the convicted murderer Lucy Letby has become deeply political with regard to whistleblowing, medical care and the role of expert witnesses.

When it comes to this latest iteration of the Lizzie Borden story, the Netflix show appears to make a connection between Borden and 20th-century serial killer Aileen Wuornos, who received her own Hollywood treatment in a film starring Charlize Theron , also called Monster. This seems designed to, as the publicity materials state, tap into a “ legacy of female rage ” and provide an “exploration of why women kill”. From the opening episode, the show takes a highly sexualised and graphic approach to the story of the killings.

Was Borden guilty? We may never know. What we do know is that there were four people in the Borden household on the morning of 4 August 1892: Andrew Borden, Abby Borden, Lizzie Borden and Bridget Sullivan. By lunchtime, Andrew and Abby were hacked to death; Abby’s body was abandoned face-down on a bedroom floor and Andrew’s lay on a blood-drenched sofa. The brutal reality is that this was a horrific crime – whether a result of “female rage” or not.

Rebecca Rideal is a historian and the author of 1666: Plague, War and Hellfire . She co-hosts the historical true-crime podcast series Buried Evidence , and writes on history, true crime and culture
