editorials.title: Australia has done precious little to prepare for the dangers of AI. Where is brilliant leadership when you need it?
editorials.passage:
There’s nothing like a threat of human extinction to focus the mind.

The threat of AI to the existence of humanity has long been raised.

But with the rapid mainstreaming of artificial intelligence, warnings from three researchers from Anthropic have landed differently, with the prediction that the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.

As if people didn’t have enough to worry about with the cost of living, shortage of housing, the climate crisis, resulting escalating mental health problems, the drift to rightwing populism and fraying of democracy, now this.

If the expected question from the grandkids was “What did you do when the world was burning and democracy was failing?”, it’s now “What did you do when we got to the brink of outsmarting ourselves out of existence?”

There are deep community concerns about datacentres, jobs and livelihoods, privacy and the very future of human creativity. Tech journalists are already claiming AI agents are “harassing people, making spam and sales calls, deleting your inbox, cancelling flights, giving control of Instagram accounts to hackers, deleting companies’ databases, filling music streaming platforms with slop, hacking companies, running scams, and snatching up dinner reservations. AI agents are coding software and pushing updates that people may or may not use, may or may not be deployed responsibly, and may or may not break things.”

The Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, has warned that rogue AI agents, like those from OpenAI that escaped their test environment in July, are “capable of taking over the entire internet” within six to 12 months.

Agentic AI is also capable of doing much good, including, among other things, identifying network vulnerabilities, responding nimbly to threats and threading knowledge across sectors.

And while much of the focus is on the risks that AI poses to democracy, there is immense potential to use it to increase community engagement and participation if deployed well.

It’s the risk/reward matrix that’s at the core of the policy and regulation struggle around data, mis- and disinformation and community trust, national security and finance, as well as the overall impact on communities, for good and bad.

A new study from MIT FutureTech and the University of Queensland identifies five risks as the most likely to produce the most severe harms; dangerous capabilities, competitive pressures, weapons and cyber-attacks, concentrated power and false information: “Under the business-as-usual scenario, experts judged that 18 of the 24 AI risk domains had at least a 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes over the next five years.”

The researchers emphasise the need to treat AI as a new paradigm with “ecosystem-wide, society-wide opportunities and vulnerabilities.”

The Albanese government has recently taken some initial steps but, as Western Australian independent Kate Chaney notes in her recent discussion paper on AI, Australia has done “remarkably little to prepare” not for what’s coming but what’s already here.

Several nations are attempting to transition to their own “native” systems amid concerns that a “kill switch” could be deployed as a weapon. This could crash economies and cause untold death and destruction by shutting down healthcare, education, transport, energy and all other communications reliant systems.

One of my definitive reflections on covering disasters as a foreign correspondent is that once the communications fail all other systems break down, including law and order. This threat is dire.

In the UK, there are calls for a new, multinational AI treaty.

OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has said: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”

The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, is a proponent of stronger alliances between middle powers. He is advocating for cooperation with like-minded democracies to avoid dependence on global tech companies, through “strategic autonomy”.

The US president, Donald Trump, meanwhile, who will meet the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, in Washington this week, says: “We’re leading China on AI … and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”

Right now, more than 30% of the US Standard and Poor’s top 500 index sits with a handful of tech companies. Nvidia alone represents 8% of the S&P.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing to list on the Nasdaq.

If ever we needed sensible, collaborative and timely leadership, it’s now.

There is no other option but to proactively and thoughtfully manage both the risks and opportunities that come with what looks to be the most significant technological development since the splitting of the atom in the 1930s. That brought with it both profound benefits and mass destruction.

And, if you thought the world was already ruled by the tech bros, it’s about to go nuclear.

Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for Goldstein

editorials.title: By fixating on immigration numbers, are our leaders missing the bigger picture for working Australians?
editorials.passage:
W hen the immigration minister, Tony Burke , approached the National Press Club podium on Thursday, the eyes of every migrant in the country would have been fixed on him. But, in fact, Burke’s address was a message for all working people across the country – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us.

The past 12 months have seen all sides of politics cohere around the consensus articulated in the introduction to Burke’s address by the press club’s president, Tom Connell: “there is furious agreement over a need for a cut to immigration.” The only difference across the political spectrum is in the detail: who deserves to be cut, and who is valuable or otherwise deserving enough to remain.

In fact, judging by the tenor of current debate, it would be easy to think that immigration is the only economic lever available to the government to address housing affordability, falling wages and cost-of-living pressures. To test that theory, consider whether, over a Sunday lunch, your uncle is more likely to proffer an opinion on tax settings driving housing speculation, the corporate supermarket duopoly or immigration levels? There is an attractively simple supply-and-demand logic underlying the assumption that fewer people will automatically mean more to go around.

But migrants didn’t design – and then implement over 20 years – the tax breaks that transformed housing into an asset , allowing investors to drive up prices and control distribution through property hoarding. And it wasn’t migrants, sitting in state and federal legislatures, who chose to wind back investment in public housing that previous generations had benefited from.

Migrants didn’t mastermind the attacks on collective bargaining that have seen union membership and real wages plummet over the past two decades. And they didn’t invent the supermarket duopoly or dictate the eye-watering profits that Coles and Woolworths maintain, driving up grocery prices while wages remain stagnant .

But as long as public debate remains fixated on immigration numbers, the bigger policy questions that could actually transform the lives of working people will remain unanswered. And there will be an endless, self-fulfilling cycle of blame targeting our friends, neighbours and co-workers born overseas for problems not of their making.

Burke set the scene for future blame-shifting. Design features of our migration program are ascribed to temporary migrants as a kind of collective moral failing. For decades, governments have re-geared the migration system towards temporary migration and shifted the goalposts on permanent residency. The natural result of this – that people transition between temporary visas to realise their hopes of permanent migration – has been recast as an illegitimate form of “visa-hopping”.

International students and graduates will no longer be able to migrate with their partners and children because, according to Burke, they should not receive special treatment compared with permanent residents and citizens forced to wait years for family reunion. But family visa processing blowouts are the direct result of ministerial directions that deprioritise and slow down some applications .

The path has been cleared for more “comprehensive” measures to come, when political and economic pressures demand them. The government has repeatedly floated the idea of legislating a 30-day window on asylum applications, requiring new migrants to make a claim immediately or miss out. This would, of course, force people seeking asylum who have missed the eligibility window to remain in the community without a visa, exposing them either to destitution, exploitative work in the cash economy or being rounded up in immigration raids.

As tempting as it might be to blame grievance politics, far-right organising or the electoral rise of One Nation for the current impasse, these are just symptoms of a much deeper malaise. It will always be in the interests of our political leaders and their backers to deflect blame for economic conditions away from themselves and on to people who cannot speak back at the ballot box.

By continuing to allow immigration to be the scapegoat for economic grievance, we not only abandon refugees and migrants to endless cycles of blame – we abandon working people to the very conditions that produced the grievances in the first place.

Sanmati Verma is the legal director of the migration justice program at the Human Rights Law Centre

editorials.title: Africa’s Green Revolution threatens traditional foods
editorials.passage:
This year, AGRA, the donor-funded agricultural development initiative formerly known as the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, is celebrating its 20th anniversary.

AGRA’s slogan is “sustainably growing Africa’s food systems”, but for years, researchers and farmers have warned that the policies it promotes are having a negative impact on African agriculture.

Our new research provides more evidence to that effect. We have documented how AGRA’s Green Revolution, with its well-funded promotion of commercial seeds, fertilisers and other inputs, has failed to spur the “productivity revolution” promised by its founders.

Worse still, its promotion of monocultures, such as maize, has led to the massive expansion of land dedicated to them. At the same time, more resilient and nutritious local crops, such as millet, are losing ground.

Hunger continues to increase in Africa, driven by climate change, desertification, conflict and disruptions to international supply lines from international conflicts like the Ukraine war. The Green Revolution promoted by AGRA does not seem to have made much of a difference.

In countries where AGRA has had significant presence, the number of undernourished people has increased by about 60 percent – roughly the same rate as the rest of the continent.

The United Nations is calling for greater attention to “affordable healthy diets”. For Africa’s small-scale farmers, who grow what their families and communities eat, that means more, not less, crop diversity, which is the opposite of what the Green Revolution has produced.

In countries that have participated in AGRA projects, crops such as maize are promoted and funded with billions of dollars in subsidies and investment. Despite that, yields for maize have grown only modestly, just 40 percent over 18 years, well below the 100 percent improvement promised by AGRA.

Some countries, like Malawi and Ethiopia, have seen stronger yield growth for maize, but some, such as Kenya – where AGRA’s headquarters are located – have seen yields decline.

Maize production has soared across participant countries, driven mainly by the massive expansion of plantings as subsidies drive farmers to plant maize on new land.

In contrast, our research shows that traditional African staples such as sorghum, cassava, and groundnuts have lost land and investment. Since AGRA was launched in 2006, 13 countries that have participated have seen a decline in productivity of 21 percent for cassava and 10 percent for groundnuts in total.

But millet – a climate-resilient, nutritious grain – is the crop that has suffered the most. Before 2006, millet was as prevalent as maize in these countries. Since 2006, millet production has fallen 27 percent, while maize production has more than doubled. Millet yields have fallen 17 percent with the lack of investment. And as land allocated to maize production increased 71 percent, land for millet fell 12 percent.

Millet is not some backward crop waiting to be replaced by maize. For generations, it has fed communities across some of Africa’s driest regions. It can withstand heat and drought, grow with relatively few external inputs, and provide nutritious food where other crops struggle.

In 2023, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) celebrated the “Year of Millets”, highlighting the multiple benefits of the crop to the environment and social welfare.

The same is true of many of Africa’s traditional crops – sorghum, fonio, cowpeas, cassava, indigenous vegetables and many others. They are part of the biological diversity of African farming, but also of our cuisines, knowledge and cultures.

At a time of climate change, pushing such crops aside makes particularly little sense. Farmers need more options in their fields, not fewer. A diverse farm spreads risk: when one crop suffers from drought, pests or disease, another may survive. Rotation and diversity of crops help keep soils more fertile.

Rhetorically, AGRA now professes to value the very crops that its Green Revolution helped push to the margins. It speaks of diverse, nutritious and climate-adapted crops, and its seed programmes include millet, sorghum, cowpea, groundnut and others.

We welcome serious investment in these crops. It is overdue. But there is no indication that AGRA and other Green Revolution proponents will abandon their chosen monocrops, such as maize. AGRA’s current seed strategy still emphasises improved varieties, certified seeds, faster variety turnover, commercialisation and market-oriented seed systems.

Investment needs to support farmers’ rights to save, use, exchange and develop their seeds, protect crop diversity and indigenous knowledge, and ensure that farmers and communities – not seed markets alone – determine which varieties survive and spread.

African farmers do not need saving, but their crops – millet, sorghum, cowpea, fonio, and other traditional crops need to be rescued from Green Revolution crop-breeders.

When a traditional crop disappears from farmers’ fields, we can lose locally adapted seed varieties, knowledge about how to grow and prepare them and foods that are central to local diets and identities.

This is why the decline of millet should concern us far beyond the millet field. Africa is already dangerously exposed to climate shocks and volatile international food and fertiliser markets. Diversity is one of our greatest protections against those risks. Yet we are subsidising its disappearance.

It is not enough for the UN to call for greater access for all to nutritious diets. For the majority of Africa’s rural populations, who are also among its least food-secure, crop diversity is key to diet diversity. It is time for AGRA, the African Development Bank, foreign donors and African governments to stop subsidising and promoting the crops that are driving the loss of such diversity.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Police hiring standards matter. But they alone cannot stop abuse
editorials.passage:
During a congressional hearing earlier this week, FBI Director Kash Patel defended changes to the bureau’s hiring standards. His testimony came just two weeks after reports surfaced of loosened hiring standards at another law enforcement agency in the US: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

As a result, concerns have emerged about a retreat from standards intended to protect the public by offering a baseline of conduct for law enforcement officers. The American public is right to worry. Loose hiring standards can put reckless individuals in positions of power.

But ensuring commitment to higher standards in law enforcement recruitment alone cannot solve the police violence problem in the US.

Research on police misconduct, which has considerably expanded in the wake of Black Lives Matter and related movements, offers useful parameters to guide how we approach the question of hiring standards.

Studies have shown that most cases of use of force are concentrated among a relatively small proportion of officers, at least in the limited departments that track such incidents. That means there are officers who are repeat offenders and have the tendency to engage in such misconduct.

So can risk individuals be identified before they are hired?

One study of more than 12,000 police applicants found that specific responses on pre-employment psychological evaluations were associated with subsequent excessive force complaints and complaints alleging racial misconduct.

However, another study of 642 first-year police officers found that markers for anti-social and borderline behaviour could predict the likelihood of engaging only in certain types of abuse – namely sexual misconduct.

There is also research that suggests abusive policing and officers’ psychological wellbeing may be intertwined, and that the harms of misconduct may extend beyond targeted civilians, possibly even to the offending officers themselves.

In a sample of 137 active-duty US police officers, approximately 11 percent self-reported engaging in abusive policing. Abusive policing was associated with greater PTSD symptoms even after accounting for adverse childhood experiences and workplace trauma.

The implication of all this is that hiring standards based on psychological profiling should neither be dismissed as irrelevant nor treated as a fully reliable way to eliminate all future risk. Standards should be evaluated according to what they actually predict, what they exclude, and what risks arise when they are removed.

But improper selection of law enforcement recruits is only part of the problem.

The US has an exceptionally high rate of police violence compared with other wealthy democracies. For example, the rate of police killings is 33.5 per 10 million in the US, compared with 9.8 in Canada, 1.3 in Germany, and 0.5 in England and Wales.

That cannot plausibly be explained simply by whom we happen to hire. American law enforcement gives officers extraordinary authority to detain, search, use force and, in some circumstances, take a life.

Those powers operate within institutions that have repeatedly struggled with racial bias, unnecessary antagonism of marginalised communities, and abuses of authority. There is also inadequate accountability for law enforcement misconduct, including through qualified immunity and other legal protections that can make it difficult to hold officers personally liable for certain constitutional violations.

The problem, in other words, is not simply that some individuals enter policing who should not. It is also the system into which they enter, and the organisational cultures, incentives, and practices that can shape how they use the power they have been given.

Reducing police misconduct requires system-wide reform, including greater accountability not only for individual officers but for the agencies and institutions responsible for policing.

Effective policing depends in part on public cooperation. Global research across dozens of countries has linked perceived fairness, procedural justice and trust in police to people’s willingness to cooperate with law enforcement.

The credibility of hiring standards can be part of trust-building initiatives, but they must also include broader efforts to strengthen trust and legitimacy among marginalised communities by reducing racial profiling, unnecessary uses of force, and inequitable enforcement of laws.

The challenge is not simply to identify the “wrong” candidates and exclude them, but to build institutions in which selection is accompanied by effective training, supervision, and accountability. Ultimately, the institutions entrusted with extraordinary powers have to be structured to protect the people they serve.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: How I would like Indians to discover Poland—pierogi, Chopin, friendship: Polish Ambassador
editorials.passage:
F irst, let me put Poland on the map. For many Indians, Poland is still a country somewhere in Europe, quite a long way away, but perhaps not exactly where one would first choose to go on a European holiday. When Indians think of Europe, they usually think of France, Britain, Italy, or Switzerland. Poland is not often among their first choices. I would like to change that.

F irst, let me put Poland on the map.

For many Indians, Poland is still a country somewhere in Europe, quite a long way away, but perhaps not exactly where one would first choose to go on a European holiday. When Indians think of Europe, they usually think of France, Britain, Italy, or Switzerland. Poland is not often among their first choices. I would like to change that.

For many Indians, Poland is still a country somewhere in Europe, quite a long way away, but perhaps not exactly where one would first choose to go on a European holiday.

When Indians think of Europe, they usually think of France, Britain, Italy, or Switzerland. Poland is not often among their first choices. I would like to change that.

Poland today is a different country from the one many people may remember from history books. We are the sixth-largest economy in the European Union, the 20th largest economy in the world, with a GDP of $ 1 trillion . O ver the past 35 years, Poland has experienced one of the most remarkable periods of economic growth in modern Europe. For India, this makes Poland particularly interesting. India is one of the world’s great rising powers, and Poland is increasingly becoming one of Europe’s important economic and strategic powers. There are many opportunities for our two countries to do more business, invest, study, and work together. T here is one more advantage: Poland is still relatively affordable by Western European standards. Our cities are clean and safe, and Warsaw is one of Europe’s safer capitals. But I would argue that Poland’s greatest advantage for an Indian visitor is something that does not appear in any economic statistic: Indians are very popular in Poland. Indians are already winning hearts India has an extraordinarily positive image among Poles. Ask a Pole about India and, very often, you will hear about yoga, Bollywood, spirituality, and food. In fact, Indian restaurants have become so popular that the cuisine is one of the most visible foreign food cultures in Poland. The interest goes both ways. Increasing numbers of Indians are coming to Poland to study, work, and build businesses. There is a growing Indian community, and while I cannot claim that every Pole gets up at sunrise to practice yoga, I can assure you that it is very much a success story in Poland. There are also some fascinating linguistic and cultural connections between India and Poland. Sanskrit and Hindi have fascinated Polish scholars for generations. I would like my Indian friends to think of Poland not as a distant corner of Europe, but as a friendly gateway to the continent . Also read: I started liking paneer in India. Shahi paneer is my favourite now: Polish Ambassador If you want to understand Poland, read us Poland takes literature rather seriously. Perhaps this is because, during difficult periods in our history, literature was one of the ways we preserved our national identity. We have had six Nobel laureates in l iterature—Henryk Sienkiewicz, Władysław Reymont, Isaac Bashevis Singer, Czesław Miłosz, Wisława Szymborska, and Olga Tokarczuk. Our most recent laureate, Tokarczuk, won the Nobel Prize in 2018. Tokarczuk is a writer I would particularly recommend to Indian readers because she is fascinated by movement between cultures, travel, memory, and identity. Her Flights (2007) is about travelling itself, which seems appropriate for anyone thinking about travelling from India to Poland. But if you ask me for my favourite author , I would name Bruno Schulz. He was a wonderfully strange writer who took the ordinary world around him—a small Polish town, family life, shops, streets—and turned it into something almost mythical. In The Street of Crocodiles (1934) , reality and fantasy constantly change places. I like writers who remind us that the world is stranger than we think. Schulz certainly does that. For something more contemporary, I would recommend Andrzej Sapkowski, author of The Witcher saga. Many Indians may know The Witcher first from Netflix or the enormously successful video games. But before Geralt of Rivia became a global celebrity, he was a character created by a Polish writer. And beneath all the monsters, magic, and sword fights, Sapkowski is actually asking very serious questions about prejudice, power, morality, and what makes someone a hero. Among Polish poets, one of my favourites is Marcin Świetlicki. His poetry is urban, ironic, and sometimes wonderfully dark. His collection Night Truck Driver (2020) has recently become available in English, giving English-speaking readers a chance to discover his distinctive voice. I f you want to understand Poland beyond the tourist brochures, I would say, read us. T ry Polish food Now we come to a subject on which every Polish person becomes an expert : food. I will admit that Polish cuisine is not exactly famous for being light. If you are looking for a cuisine based on salads and gentle portions, Poland may require some preparation. Our traditional food was developed in a climate where winter means winter. So we have potatoes, cabbage, meat, mushrooms, dumplings, and soups substantial enough to survive a snowstorm. In fact, I think soups are one of the most interesting parts of Polish cuisine. We have żurek (a sour rye soup), rosół (traditional chicken broth), and barszcz czerwony (beetroot soup). S ome of our dishes require a certain amount of courage. There is milk soup and fruit soup. However, the ultimate test of whether you are Polish is czernina, a traditional duck-blood soup. It is not for everyone , to say the least. For Indian vegetarian visitors, my recommendation would be pierogi ruskie, dumplings traditionally filled with potato and cheese, and our excellent potato pancakes. Pierogi are particularly interesting because they are not simply food. They are part of Polish family culture. Every Polish grandmother seems to have her own recipe, and every family believes, naturally, that their grandmother makes the best pierogi. And if you want something less formal, try a zapiekanka. It is essentially a toasted piece of baguette with mushrooms and melted cheese, usually covered with ketchup. It sounds simple, and it is . My travel recommendations If I had to recommend one destination to an Indian visitor, I would choose Kraków. It is one of the best places to experience the layers of Polish history and culture in a compact and beautiful setting. Its medieval Old Town, Wawel Castle, churches, cafés, and lively cultural life make it an ideal starting point. From Kraków, one can also easily explore southern Poland and the Tatra Mountains, with their beautiful alpine landscapes. If you like the sea, go north to Gdańsk and the Baltic coast. If you like lakes, forests, and quiet landscapes, visit the Masurian Lake District. If you like medieval architecture, visit Malbork, home to one of the largest medieval castles in the world. And if you want something truly wild, go to the Białowieża Forest in the northeast. It is one of Europe’s last great primaeval forests and home to the European bison. Also read: Andes to Amazon—here’s how Indian travellers can experience Ecuador: Ecuadorian Ambassador Polish music is not just music Music is another essential part of my life. I listen to music for more than 10 hours a day. I find it difficult to work or even read without music. Naturally, if you talk about Polish music, you have to begin with Frédéric Chopin. I often tell people: if you want to understand Poland and the Polish character, listen to Chopin. His music contains extraordinary beauty, but also drama and longing. Perhaps this should not surprise us. Poland has experienced enough history to give a nation a very complicated relationship with happiness. But Chopin is only the beginning. We have produced outstanding 20 th-century composers such as Karol Szymanowski and Krzysztof Penderecki, and Poland has developed one of Europe’s most distinctive jazz traditions. If I had to introduce one Polish jazz musician to Indian audiences, I would choose Krzysztof Komeda. Komeda was an extraordinary musician and composer who helped create the distinctive Polish jazz sound. He also worked with Roman Polański on several films, most famously Rosemary’s Baby (1968) . The lullaby from Rosemary’s Baby —‘Sleep Safe and Warm’—is one of those melodies that you may recognise without even knowing where you heard it. Komeda’s story is also a good example of what I find fascinating about Polish culture. We have always absorbed influences from elsewhere and then transformed them into something of our own. That brings me to contemporary music. Polish pop music has not conquered the world in quite the way that American or British pop has. Perhaps we are simply too original. Or perhaps we have not yet found the right marketing department! But there are musicians creating interesting connections between Poland and India. One of them is Michał Rudaś, who has a particular interest in Indian music and culture. His work has brought Polish and Indian musical traditions into conversation with one another. T he fact remains that the best way to discover a country is not through statistics, monuments, or even guidebooks, but through the small experiences that stay with you: a conversation over coffee, a plate of pierogi, a Chopin melody, a walk through an old city, or an unexpected friendship. Poland may still be far away from India geographically, but I hope that more Indians will discover how close our two countries can feel in spirit. Come to Poland with curiosity — not only as visitors, but as friends. You may arrive looking for Europe and leave having discovered Poland. Poland today is a different country from the one many people may remember from history books. We are the sixth-largest economy in the European Union, the 20th largest economy in the world, with a GDP of $ 1 trillion . O ver the past 35 years, Poland has experienced one of the most remarkable periods of economic growth in modern Europe.

For India, this makes Poland particularly interesting. India is one of the world’s great rising powers, and Poland is increasingly becoming one of Europe’s important economic and strategic powers. There are many opportunities for our two countries to do more business, invest, study, and work together. T here is one more advantage: Poland is still relatively affordable by Western European standards. Our cities are clean and safe, and Warsaw is one of Europe’s safer capitals. But I would argue that Poland’s greatest advantage for an Indian visitor is something that does not appear in any economic statistic: Indians are very popular in Poland. Indians are already winning hearts India has an extraordinarily positive image among Poles. Ask a Pole about India and, very often, you will hear about yoga, Bollywood, spirituality, and food. Increasing numbers of Indians are coming to Poland to study, work, and build businesses. There is a growing Indian community, and while I cannot claim that every Pole gets up at sunrise to practice yoga, I can assure you that it is very much a success story in Poland. editorials.title: Does robotic hair transplant really work for women?
editorials.passage:
H air loss is something I increasingly see women seeking help for. N ot just because their hair is thinning, but because of what it does to their self- confidence. A widening parting, a receding hairline or a visible scalp can be surprisingly distressing, particularly for women who have spent years thinking that hair transplantation was primarily a treatment for men. Today, one term that comes up frequently in my consultations is robotic hair transplantation. Patients often ask me: “Doctor, is robotic hair transplant actually better? And can it work for women?”

H air loss is something I increasingly see women seeking help for. N ot just because their hair is thinning, but because of what it does to their self- confidence. A widening parting, a receding hairline or a visible scalp can be surprisingly distressing, particularly for women who have spent years thinking that hair transplantation was primarily a treatment for men.

Today, one term that comes up frequently in my consultations is robotic hair transplantation. Patients often ask me: “Doctor, is robotic hair transplant actually better? And can it work for women?”

Today, one term that comes up frequently in my consultations is robotic hair transplantation.

Patients often ask me: “Doctor, is robotic hair transplant actually better? And can it work for women?”

My answer is simple: it can work for selected women, but the word “robotic” should not be mistaken for “better.” So, what exactly is a robotic hair transplant? Robotic hair transplantation is essentially a technology-assisted form of Follicular Unit Extraction, or FUE. In conventional FUE, individual follicular units are carefully extracted from the donor area. These grafts are then prepared and transplanted into areas where the hair is thinning. With robotic transplants , sophisticated imaging and computer assis tance help identify suitable follicular units and assist in their extraction. But there is one thing I always tell my patients: the robot does not replace the hair-transplant surgeon. The most important decisions still require clinical judgement. Which woman is actually a candidate? How stable is her hair loss? Is her donor area strong enough? How many grafts are required? Where should they be placed? How should the hairline or parting be designed? These are not decisions that should be handed over to a machine. But does it then make robotics better? Not automatically. There is an understandable excitement around robotics because it can provide greater consistency and can assist in the transplant process . But a successful hair transplant is much more than extracting grafts. I have seen patients become very focused on the machine being used, when what really matters is the diagnosis, donor quality, surgical planning, graft handling and, ultimately, whether the procedure is appropriate for that particular person. The published evidence comparing robotic and conventional FUE is still relatively limited, particularly for women. Some studies have found broadly comparable outcomes between robotic and conventional techniques, but these studies are small and cannot simply be applied to every female patient. This is why I would be cautious about making sweeping claims that robotic transplantation is superior. Also Read: Exosomes are the latest buzzword in hair loss treatments. Do they work for everyone? Why is hair transplantation particularly challenging in women? This is where the conversation becomes much more interesting. Female hair loss is often different from the classic male pattern baldness. Many women develop diffuse thinning, particularly around the central scalp and crown, rather than developing a clearly defined bald patch.

And sometimes, the donor area itself may have early thinning. That creates a major problem. You cannot build a beautiful transplant using hair that is itself progressively becoming weak. This is why I strongly believe that diagnosis must come before transplantation. Before considering surgery, I want to understand why the woman is losing hair. Is it female-pattern hair loss? Chronic telogen effluvium? Nutritional deficiency? A thyroid problem? A hormonal issue? Traction? Or, in some cases, a scarring form of alopecia? Sometimes the right treatment is not surgery at all. And more often than not, stabilising the hair loss medically can make the eventual surgical result much more predictable. Who benefits and who doesn’t A woman may be considered a suitable candidate when her hair loss is relatively stable, the donor area has adequate density and stability, there is a clearly identifiable area where additional hair would make a meaningful cosmetic difference, and she has realistic expectations. I particularly like to assess the donor area carefully with trichoscopy before discussing transplantation. For me, this is one of the most important steps. A woman may walk into my clinic saying, “I want a hair transplant,” but a good dermatologist does not simply to agree. As her doctor, m y job is to determine whether a transplant is likely to be useful and sustainable for her. But the biggest misconception that most women have is that a transplant stops hair loss. This is probably the single most important point I would want women to understand. A transplanted follicle may be relatively resistant to hair loss because it comes from a stable donor zone. But the original hair that was already present on the scalp can continue to thin. So a transplant is not necessarily the end of hair-loss treatment. In many women, medical treatment may still be required to preserve their existing hair. I often explain it this way: the goal is not simply to add hair. The goal is to preserve the hair you have and strategically add hair where it will make the greatest visual difference. That is what creates a natural-looking result over time. Also Read: Hair loss drugs are the next Ozempic. Biotech stocks are climbing What can a woman realistically expect? Hair transplantation requires patience. The transplanted hair does not simply appear the next morning. The follicles go through a period of shedding before new growth gradually begins. Visible improvement develops over several months, and the final result is generally assessed around nine to twelve months. However, the goal for a woman is often quite different than for a man . We may not be trying to create a completely dense scalp. Sometimes a relatively small number of strategically placed grafts can make a significant difference—particularly around the frontal hairline, a widening central parting or an area where the scalp has become visibly prominent. In women, strategic density can be more important than simply chasing numbers of grafts. Is robotic hair transplant the future? I certainly think robotics and artificial intelligence have an interesting role to play in hair restoration. As imaging improves and technology becomes more precise, robotic assistance may become increasingly useful. But I would not want women to choose a transplant simply because the procedure is described as “robotic”. The machine is only one component of the treatment. For me, the most important technology is still good diagnosis, detailed trichoscopy, careful donor assessment and an understanding of female hair biology. A robot can assist in extracting a follicle. It cannot decide whether that woman should have a transplant in the first place. And that decision remains the most important part of the entire treatment. editorials.title: India has the technology to end extreme hunger now. It’s a question of public will
editorials.passage:
E very political order rests on a fiction that must be renewed continuously, or it dies. Jean-Jacques Rousseau called it the social contract, and he was careful to note that it is not a document but a disposition. The general will remains general only so long as each subject internalises it as their own. That internalisation is personal morality: not obedience to law, but the mechanism by which an external political arrangement becomes an interior fact, felt as legitimate rather than imposed. Morality is the load-bearing wall between the political order and the subject, the thing that keeps the contract valid once the founders are dead and the reasons for the arrangement have faded into habit. This is why technology and political revolution resist being understood as one term acting upon another, as though technology were a tool revolutionaries pick up and revolution a response technology triggers. Each new technological regime reconstitutes the conditions under which a subject can be said to consent at all: what they can know, whom they can address, which forms of coercion are visible, and which are ambient enough to escape notice. When those conditions change, the old morality stops performing its function. It no longer makes the citizen feel that the general will is theirs. A gap opens between the political order and the subject, and that gap is where revolutions live. A revolution that changes the political order without closing that gap has not renewed the contract. It has relocated the crisis.

A gap opens between the political order and the subject, and that gap is where revolutions live. A revolution that changes the political order without closing that gap has not renewed the contract. It has relocated the crisis.

Three precedents The printing press did this once. It dissolved the Church’s monopoly on textual authority, made vernacular scripture and pamphlet argument available to anyone literate enough to read them, and forced into existence a moral vocabulary capable of legitimating a post-clerical order: conscience, private judg e ment, the individual reader answerable to g od without an intermediary. That vocabulary arrived because clerical mediation stopped working the instant print made it optional, and something had to fill the gap. The factory did it again, more brutally. It manufactured, in one motion, an industrial working class and the conditions that turned that class into a political subject rather than a scattered population of labourers: concentration, common grievance, shared time-discipline. What it did not supply was the moral language to explain what was owed to that new subject. Liberalism and socialism competed for a century to write it, rights against exploitation on one side, the abolition of wage labour on the other, both attempting the same Rousseauian labour: making an industrial population feel that the order under which it lived was its own general will and not merely a system it was compelled to serve. Nuclear weapons did something stranger. They created a new class of political fact rather than a new class of subject: mutual vulnerability at civilisational scale, for which the older vocabulary of just war and raison d’état had no precedent. The result was decades of improvised moral theory: deterrence ethics, non-proliferation as binding norm, the doctrine that certain weapons must be built so that they are never used. All of it was invented because the technology had outrun the inherited categories for judging political violence. Also read: Indians employ a unique mechanism to marry science and faith. It leaves both hollow The present regime Digital infrastructure is doing this now, and at the level of the state it has produced technonationalism . It is t he doctrine that sovereignty must be redefined around control of semiconductors, data flows, satellite constellations, and frontier AI models, on the reasoning that a nation which does not own its computational substrate cannot be said to own its politics. Washington’s chip export controls, Beijing’s drive toward indigenous fabrication, Brussels’s attempts to legislate data sovereignty into existence, and India’s own turn toward domestic semiconductor capacity, launch systems, and AI stacks are one story told in four accents. Each makes the same claim: dependency on another polity’s technological base is a species of unfreedom, because it leaves the conditions of one’s own deliberation in someone else’s hands. Technonationalism is a moral claim wearing the language of industrial strategy. It asserts that a people cannot author its own contract while its technological base is rented from elsewhere, and that a nation governed by infrastructure it does not control is a nation whose consent is manufactured for it. The claim is Rousseauian to its core, and India’s version deserves to be met on those terms rather than waved away as protectionism or borrowed great-power posturing. A state that must ask permission, in effect, for the chips that run its elections, its banks, and its hospitals is exposed to having its deliberation captured by whoever holds the permission. The instinct to close that exposure is neither irrational nor novel; it is the instinct that made Rousseau insist that a people subject to another’s will in the essentials of its own reproduction has not achieved political existence. But a moral claim in the language of sovereignty is not yet a moral revolution, and the honesty of this argument lives in the distance between the two. Technonationalism can produce a more capable state and leave a more moral one entirely unbuilt: the old hierarchy in new clothing, the nation-state reasserting itself through silicon and satellites while leaving untouched who, within the nation, actually benefits from the capacity reclaimed. A fabrication plant does not distribute its benefits by its own logic. A satellite constellation does not decide of its own accord to serve famine-relief logistics rather than surveillance. Those are choices, made or deferred by political subjects whose morality either does or does not demand them. The first century of the industrial revolution is the plain precedent: enormous new productive capacity coexisting for decades with a moral order that still treated most of the population it depended on as barely eligible to vote, let alone to claim a share of the surplus. The question we keep deferring That gap between capacity and obligation has a specific name in our moment: hunger. So the deferred question has to be put directly. Can the technical capacity now assembled actually eliminate mass poverty and extreme hunger within a generation? Precision agriculture, biometric cash-transfer infrastructure, cold-chain vaccine logistics, satellite-guided last-mile distribution, desalination, drought-resistant cultivars: put together, can they end what ails humanity ? The honest answer is yes, and it would not have been honest 50 years ago. That change is the single most important fact in this age, and most public argument about technology and development is organised to avoid stating it. Our situation is no longer that of 1950, when scarcity was still partly a fact of production: yields were genuinely too low, logistics were too primitive, information about who needed what and where was too poor to act on in time. Green Revolution-era India lived inside that constraint directly. It no longer does. What remains scarce is not calories in aggregate, nor the means of moving them, nor the administrative instruments for identifying who needs them; India’s own direct-benefit-transfer architecture is proof of how far that state capacity has travelled. What remains scarce is the decision to aim the assembled capacity at that end rather than another. This is the hinge of the whole account. Distribution, at the scale we are now capable of, is a moral and political choice, not a technical constraint. That sentence was false in 1950. It is true now, and pretending otherwise is itself a moral evasion: it allows the question of will to be quietly re-described as a question of capacity, which is easier to live with and no longer accurate. The hungry are not waiting on an invention. They are waiting on a decision. Which forces the second question, one a nation building sovereign technological capacity cannot avoid, however much its rhetoric prefers to. Having established that it can, does it want to? Technonationalism, if it halts at the assertion of control, answers this implicitly and dishonestly. It aims the reclaimed capacity at strategic autonomy, prestige, and deterrence, and files the elimination of hunger under residual benefits that may or may not follow, rather than under the test against which the whole project’s legitimacy should be measured. A moral revolution would reverse the order of justification, demanding that the reclaimed capacity answer to that test first, and requiring the political subject, not merely the state or the technologist, to insist that sovereignty over technology carries responsibility for what that technology could do and currently does not. The printing press did this once. It dissolved the Church’s monopoly on textual authority, made vernacular scripture and pamphlet argument available to anyone literate enough to read them, and forced into existence a moral vocabulary capable of legitimating a post-clerical order: conscience, private judg e ment, the individual reader answerable to g od without an intermediary. That vocabulary arrived because clerical mediation stopped working the instant print made it optional, and something had to fill the gap.

The factory did it again, more brutally. It manufactured, in one motion, an industrial working class and the conditions that turned that class into a political subject rather than a scattered population of labourers: concentration, common grievance, shared time-discipline. What it did not supply was the moral language to explain what was owed to that new subject. Liberalism and socialism competed for a century to write it, rights against exploitation on one side, the abolition of wage labour on the other, both attempting the same Rousseauian labour: making an industrial population feel that the order under which it lived was its own general will and not merely a system it was compelled to serve. Nuclear weapons did something stranger. They created a new class of political fact rather than a new class of subject: mutual vulnerability at civilisational scale, for which the older vocabulary of just war and raison d’état had no precedent. The result was decades of improvised moral theory: deterrence ethics, non-proliferation as binding norm, the doctrine that certain weapons must be built so that they are never used. It leaves both hollow The present regime Digital infrastructure is doing this now, and at the level of the state it has produced technonationalism . It is t he doctrine that sovereignty must be redefined around control of semiconductors, data flows, satellite constellations, and frontier AI models, on the reasoning that a nation which does not own its computational substrate cannot be said to own its politics. Washington’s chip export controls, Beijing’s drive toward indigenous fabrication, Brussels’s attempts to legislate data sovereignty into existence, and India’s own turn toward domestic semiconductor capacity, launch systems, and AI stacks are one story told in four accents. Each makes the same claim: dependency on another polity’s technological base is a species of unfreedom, because it leaves the conditions of one’s own deliberation in someone else’s hands. Technonationalism is a moral claim wearing the language of industrial strategy. It asserts that a people cannot author its own contract while its technological base is rented from elsewhere, and that a nation governed by infrastructure it does not control is a nation whose consent is manufactured for it. The claim is Rousseauian to its core, and India’s version deserves to be met on those terms rather than waved away as protectionism or borrowed great-power posturing. A state that must ask permission, in effect, for the chips that run its elections, its banks, and its hospitals is exposed to having its deliberation captured by whoever holds the permission. The instinct to close that exposure is neither irrational nor novel; it is the instinct that made Rousseau insist that a people subject to another’s will in the essentials of its own reproduction has not achieved political existence. But a moral claim in the language of sovereignty is not yet a moral revolution, and the honesty of this argument lives in the distance between the two. Technonationalism can produce a more capable state and leave a more moral one entirely unbuilt: the old hierarchy in new clothing, the nation-state reasserting itself through silicon and satellites while leaving untouched who, within the nation, actually benefits from the capacity reclaimed. A fabrication plant does not distribute its benefits by its own logic. A satellite constellation does not decide of its own accord to serve famine-relief logistics rather than surveillance. Those are choices, made or deferred by political subjects whose morality either does or does not demand them. The first century of the industrial revolution is the plain precedent: enormous new productive capacity coexisting for decades with a moral order that still treated most of the population it depended on as barely eligible to vote, let alone to claim a share of the surplus. The honest answer is yes, and it would not have been honest 50 years ago. Our situation is no longer that of 1950, when scarcity was still partly a fact of production: yields were genuinely too low, logistics were too primitive, information about who needed what and where was too poor to act on in time. Because a state acting from strategic calculation rather than an internalised general will produces exactly the residual-benefit posture already diagnosed. Charity from above, undertaken for prestige or stability, is discretionary by nature, extended when convenient and withdrawn when the calculation shifts, answerable to no one when it is. Only an obligation internalised by subjects as constitutive of what their sovereignty was for, becomes non-negotiable, something a government can be held to have violated rather than merely declined. The second makes their feeding a condition of the contract’s legitimacy. Technonationalism supplies the will no more than the printing press supplied the doctrine of conscience or the factory supplied the labour movement. Its specific shape is a generation that could be the first in human history to end extreme hunger, holding every instrument the task requires and awaiting only the decision to use them for it. Digital infrastructure is doing this now, and at the level of the state it has produced technonationalism . It is t he doctrine that sovereignty must be redefined around control of semiconductors, data flows, satellite constellations, and frontier AI models, on the reasoning that a nation which does not own its computational substrate cannot be said to own its politics. Washington’s chip export controls, Beijing’s drive toward indigenous fabrication, Brussels’s attempts to legislate data sovereignty into existence, and India’s own turn toward domestic semiconductor capacity, launch systems, and AI stacks are one story told in four accents. Each makes the same claim: dependency on another polity’s technological base is a species of unfreedom, because it leaves the conditions of one’s own deliberation in someone else’s hands.

Technonationalism is a moral claim wearing the language of industrial strategy. It asserts that a people cannot author its own contract while its technological base is rented from elsewhere, and that a nation governed by infrastructure it does not control is a nation whose consent is manufactured for it. The claim is Rousseauian to its core, and India’s version deserves to be met on those terms rather than waved away as protectionism or borrowed great-power posturing. A state that must ask permission, in effect, for the chips that run its elections, its banks, and its hospitals is exposed to having its deliberation captured by whoever holds the permission. The instinct to close that exposure is neither irrational nor novel; it is the instinct that made Rousseau insist that a people subject to another’s will in the essentials of its own reproduction has not achieved political existence. But a moral claim in the language of sovereignty is not yet a moral revolution, and the honesty of this argument lives in the distance between the two. Technonationalism can produce a more capable state and leave a more moral one entirely unbuilt: the old hierarchy in new clothing, the nation-state reasserting itself through silicon and satellites while leaving untouched who, within the nation, actually benefits from the capacity reclaimed. A fabrication plant does not distribute its benefits by its own logic. A satellite constellation does not decide of its own accord to serve famine-relief logistics rather than surveillance. Those are choices, made or deferred by political subjects whose morality either does or does not demand them. The first century of the industrial revolution is the plain precedent: enormous new productive capacity coexisting for decades with a moral order that still treated most of the population it depended on as barely eligible to vote, let alone to claim a share of the surplus. The question we keep deferring That gap between capacity and obligation has a specific name in our moment: hunger. So the deferred question has to be put directly. Can the technical capacity now assembled actually eliminate mass poverty and extreme hunger within a generation? Precision agriculture, biometric cash-transfer infrastructure, cold-chain vaccine logistics, satellite-guided last-mile distribution, desalination, drought-resistant cultivars: put together, can they end what ails humanity ? The honest answer is yes, and it would not have been honest 50 years ago. That change is the single most important fact in this age, and most public argument about technology and development is organised to avoid stating it. Our situation is no longer that of 1950, when scarcity was still partly a fact of production: yields were genuinely too low, logistics were too primitive, information about who needed what and where was too poor to act on in time. Green Revolution-era India lived inside that constraint directly. It no longer does. What remains scarce is not calories in aggregate, nor the means of moving them, nor the administrative instruments for identifying who needs them; India’s own direct-benefit-transfer architecture is proof of how far that state capacity has travelled. What remains scarce is the decision to aim the assembled capacity at that end rather than another. This is the hinge of the whole account. Distribution, at the scale we are now capable of, is a moral and political choice, not a technical constraint. That sentence was false in 1950. It is true now, and pretending otherwise is itself a moral evasion: it allows the question of will to be quietly re-described as a question of capacity, which is easier to live with and no longer accurate. The hungry are not waiting on an invention. They are waiting on a decision. Which forces the second question, one a nation building sovereign technological capacity cannot avoid, however much its rhetoric prefers to. Having established that it can, does it want to? Technonationalism, if it halts at the assertion of control, answers this implicitly and dishonestly. It aims the reclaimed capacity at strategic autonomy, prestige, and deterrence, and files the elimination of hunger under residual benefits that may or may not follow, rather than under the test against which the whole project’s legitimacy should be measured. A moral revolution would reverse the order of justification, demanding that the reclaimed capacity answer to that test first, and requiring the political subject, not merely the state or the technologist, to insist that sovereignty over technology carries responsibility for what that technology could do and currently does not. editorials.title: New Mercedes GLC 400 electric is big, fast, and feature-loaded. It lacks one thing
editorials.passage:
T here is an eponymous title track in the 1971 Bond film Diamonds Are Forever sung in a soprano tone by Shirley Bassey . And it is the perfect song to describe some of the classic vehicles I drove around Stuttgart, Germany , last week. One of them was the legendary Mercedes-Benz W123, the internal company code for the classic Mercedes-Benz cars from the 1980s and, in a manner of speaking, the ancestor of the E-Class sedan. If you were to ask someone who grew up in the 1980s and 1990s to draw a car, let alone a Mercedes-Benz, it would most likely look like this. Large rectangular headlights, bright orange indicator lights, and the classic ‘three-box’ shape without any concession to aerodynamics. Anyway, outside the Mercedes-Benz Museum on a summer morning in Stuttgart was a line-up of classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles. Some special old S-Class sedans were there, including the W116, W126, W140, and W123.

If you were to ask someone who grew up in the 1980s and 1990s to draw a car, let alone a Mercedes-Benz, it would most likely look like this. Large rectangular headlights, bright orange indicator lights, and the classic ‘three-box’ shape without any concession to aerodynamics.

Anyway, outside the Mercedes-Benz Museum on a summer morning in Stuttgart was a line-up of classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles. Some special old S-Class sedans were there, including the W116, W126, W140, and W123.

And why did the W123 remind me of that song? Because it lasted forever and ever and ever, as Bassey sang. These were, quite literally, indestructible. There are examples that some of these cars have done over 2 million km as taxis in Europe. The 240D from 1981 that I drove only had around 72 horsepower and a basic four-speed manual gearbox. It wasn’t what one would call engaging or enthusiastic, but it worked and worked well, and was supremely comfortable. But here is the thing, I wasn’t actually in Germany to drive these old legends, I was there to drive Mercedes-Benz’ latest and greatest, the GLC 400. This battery-electric vehicle features a host of new technologies and the carmaker is hoping that this vehicle, along with the CLA I drove a few months ago, can give Mercedes’ electrification strategy a fillip, including in India. The GLC electric is being introduced in India within just six months of its launch in Europe, and this new EV will also be assembled by Mercedes-Benz at their Indian facilities at Chakan outside Pune, with several parts and components coming from domestic suppliers. Bigger and powerful The electric GLC 400 wears the same badge as the GLC 300 petrol or the 220d diesel, but it sits on a completely new platform. You can tell them apart fairly easily from the front, given the 940 backlit squares on the grille, which light up in interesting patterns. But when you step back, even the casual observer can notice that the electric version feels bigger in every respect. And it is. While India does not get the long-wheelbase Chinese model, the electric GLC 400’s wheelbase (distance between the axles) is 84 mm longer than that of the petrol variant, and the car is overall 142 mm longer. Almost all of that extra space is dedicated for rear-seat passengers and the boot. The SUV is also slightly wider, which actually makes a big difference for rear seat passengers. The new GLC gets a total of 360 kW of power from its twin motors, one on each axle, making it quite quick. That is close to 490 horsepower in old money and allows this SUV to get from 0-100 kmph in just 4.3 seconds. Unfortunately, the traffic in and around Stuttgart didn’t allow me to really give it ‘full beans’ on the unrestricted Autobahn. But I managed a modest 165-170 kmph, although you know that the GLC can do more. And when I moved off the highways and onto the twisty roads bordering the Schwarzwald, I realised the car was well balanced too. Indeed, the day after I drove the GLC 400 , I was hosted at the truly impressive Mercedes-Benz global testing facilities at Immendingen, a few hours from Stuttgart. There I could experience at least some of the immense work that went into developing the new SUV , and every other modern Mercedes-Benz. The time in the light tunnel, for example, where you could see how modern headlights are designed and tested, was fascinating. But that could be a story for another column. Now, coming back to the GLC 400, it was as far as modern electric vehicles go, an absolutely fantastic vehicle. It is loaded to the gills with technology — like the absolutely seamless 39-inch display, the ‘skylight’ panoramic roof with unique designs, and an even more evolved ambient lighting system that dances to the music playing through the superb Burmester audio system. And all of this is run on the new MB.OS operating system, developed largely by thousands of engineers sitting in Bengaluru. I wrote about the fact that every Mercedes-Benz today has a piece of India inside in a column a few years ago. And I noticed that my words were used by Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius when he addressed the SIAM conference a couple of weeks ago. Also read: India wants more cars, buses, 2-wheelers. Manufacturers are struggling to catch up Cars without a soul? But why did I start this column with the W123 instead of the GLC? Don’t get me wrong, I don’t hanker for the past. Cars today, mainly electric vehicles, are better and crucially safer than they’ve ever been, and all while being more efficient and powerful. But they lack something. It is difficult to find the right adjectives, ‘feel’ might be the best I can do. There is no ‘throttle’ on an electric vehicle right? Pressing the accelerator is pretty much like turning the speed knob for a ceiling fan. You are adjusting a resistor after all. The lack of drama, the vibrations transferred to your spine through the right foot on the accelerator pedal, and the lack of sound, in particular, just feels weird. Not wrong, but weird. I’m more used to it now than I was a few years ago, and given the situation in the Middle East, I’m ever more convinced about the need for electric vehicles. But yes, we are giving up something. So, I’m glad Mercedes-Benz Classic keeps vehicles such as the W123 in running order, because we should never forget that vehicles once also had a soul. Kushan Mitra is an automotive journalist based in New Delhi. He tweets @kushanmitra. Views are personal. (Edited by Aamaan Alam Khan)

editorials.title: Where is my romcom moment? Hollywood promised it would happen at 27
editorials.passage:
T hat 27 is the golden age is a universal truth, at least in rom-coms and sitcoms. It is the quintessential age for a heroine. She is old enough to have a career but young enough to still struggle against society’s expectations. All while panicking that she is running out of time and must figure out her love life. Friends were around 27-years-old when the show first began. Julia Roberts’ Julianne Potter in My Best Friend’s Wedding (1997) was fully prepared to sabotage a wedding because her long-time BFF, days before her 28th birthday, decided to break their pact of marrying if they were both single at 27. And it’s not just women. Twenty-seven is the coming-of-age age for men, too, at least, according to Hollywood logic. Ted Mosby is 27 in the first season of How I Met Your Mother (2005-2014), so is Adam DeMamp in Workaholics (2011-2017). And let’s not forget Leonard Hofstadter in The Big Bang Theory (2007-2019). I could go on, but you get the picture.

Ted Mosby is 27 in the first season of How I Met Your Mother (2005-2014), so is Adam DeMamp in Workaholics (2011-2017). And let’s not forget Leonard Hofstadter in The Big Bang Theory (2007-2019). I could go on, but you get the picture.

And it’s not just women. Twenty-seven is the coming-of-age age for men, too, at least, according to Hollywood logic. Ted Mosby is 27 in the first season of How I Met Your Mother (2005-2014), so is Adam DeMamp in Workaholics (2011-2017). And let’s not forget Leonard Hofstadter in The Big Bang Theory (2007-2019). I could go on, but you get the picture.

Even Katherine Heigl in 27 Dresses (2008) was willing to break up her younger sister’s wedding. Honestly, the lengths to which a 27-year-old will go to get their happily ever after are astonishing. Now, as the cuffing season hits us all in the feels, the romcoms made around these determined younglings are going to be played again and again. The unreliable protagonists dealing with the chaos of love and longing are going to be envied and emulated as well. It is not just the films and TV shows of the 1990s and 2000s in which 27 is the golden number. In Hacks (2021-2026), Ava Daniels is a 27-year-old bisexual comedian trying to salvage Deborah Vance’s image. Eleanor Shellstrop is 27 when she dies and goes to The Good Place (2016-2020). It’s an idea so well entrenched in our collective imaginations that now scores of people across social media platforms are consoling themselves that they still have time. They are not yet 27. However, on the other end of the spectrum are those of us who are of age and still waiting for a plot twist. For a generation now, we have been taught and conditioned to believe that life starts at this age. You’re somewhat financially stable, old enough to know better but still young enough for trial and error. And so, dear universe, I must ask: Where the bibbidi-bobbidi-boo is my romcom moment? When will my sitcom start? Also Read: Movies offered a fun blueprint for adulthood. I’m stuck with war, climate change & cortisol There’s a new Club 27 Rom is dead. For a while, the last frontier of modern dating—apps—is fading away. DMs are a thing of the past (it’s cringey now). And apparently having a boyfriend is so last season (blame Vogue ). But now it seems com has left the chat too. In an era of social media sensitivity, we have lost the ability to laugh at ourselves. It’s supposedly not a “good look,” whatever that means. Joy is lacking. Whimsy can be maxed; there’s a how-to for it. And all that matters is whether it is Insta-official or not. It may have begun as the firstborns of social media entered their late twenties and realised that perhaps life isn’t all that. And so the only way to cope with that horrible realisation was by consoling ourselves that it’s not too late. That you have time and that maybe your plot twist is around the corner after all. Now, though, it’s telling yourself that you’re only in your first season is the same as buying yourself a sweet treat after a long hard day. Totally worth it and universally acceptable. Twenty-seven is the prime time to rewrite your own rules and YOLO your way through life. Reinvention and self-discovery are equal measures of white-knuckle panic and pure, unadulterated high. But in the middle of all that, at the cusp of “adulthood,” there is abject fear. The pure horror of not being able to delay life, responsibilities, and the unfortunate truth that maybe you’re actually turning into your parents. Charlotte Lucas in Pride and Prejudice (2005) was definitely onto something when she said that she was 27 and frightened. “I’ve no money and no prospects. I’m already a burden to my parents,” were her exact iconic words. Honestly, same, girl, same. Views are personal. (Edited by Ratan Priya)

Charlotte Lucas in Pride and Prejudice (2005) was definitely onto something when she said that she was 27 and frightened. “I’ve no money and no prospects. I’m already a burden to my parents,” were her exact iconic words. Honestly, same, girl, same. Views are personal. (Edited by Ratan Priya)

It is not just the films and TV shows of the 1990s and 2000s in which 27 is the golden number. In Hacks (2021-2026), Ava Daniels is a 27-year-old bisexual comedian trying to salvage Deborah Vance’s image. Eleanor Shellstrop is 27 when she dies and goes to The Good Place (2016-2020).

It’s an idea so well entrenched in our collective imaginations that now scores of people across social media platforms are consoling themselves that they still have time. They are not yet 27. However, on the other end of the spectrum are those of us who are of age and still waiting for a plot twist. For a generation now, we have been taught and conditioned to believe that life starts at this age. You’re somewhat financially stable, old enough to know better but still young enough for trial and error. And so, dear universe, I must ask: Where the bibbidi-bobbidi-boo is my romcom moment?
