editorials.title: ‘The act of writing is un-citizenly’: Amit Chaudhuri talks about his new novel, ‘Château Rouge’
editorials.passage:
In Amit Chaudhuri’s ninth novel, Château Rouge , an Indian writer arriving in Paris for a fellowship finds himself in a sublet apartment in Château Rouge, a dense, multicultural quarter sometimes called “Little Africa.” It is not the storied Paris of “Proust’s house and Baldwin’s digs,” of monuments and cafes, nor does it resemble the kind of Parisian grime popularised across the literature and myth around the city. Disconcerted, he fusses over the noise and the dirty pavements, and the various faults in the furniture of his apartment. Though part of him craves a familiar Parisian experience, he is daunted by the prospect of living out clichés, and puts off reading his long-held copy of A Moveable Feast , which is a decades-old present from his wife. But she hands him another gift: the suggestion that Hemingway had no “Hemingway’s Paris” to fall back on when he was there, and might as well have been living in a place like Château Rouge.

Emboldened by this realisation, he begins to chart a renewed path through Paris, via everyday sights and sounds he encounters whilst loitering in the neighbourhood. Through these details – comparisons of various French grocery stores, the opinions of Bangladeshi peanut sellers, spats with the fellowship admin – there emerges an unlikely experience of the fabled city. Château Rouge tussles with the necessity, and the impossibility, of experiencing a place on one’s own terms.

In a conversation with Scroll , Chaudhuri reflected on the limits and possibilities offered by history and form, his own writing practice, and on Château Rouge . Excerpts from the interview:

I wanted to start by asking you about your experience of writing this novel, especially since Château Rouge repeatedly draws attention to the act of writing or recounting a novel much like itself. I also hear that the idea for the novel came to you during a writing residency you attended. You’re right – it was almost eight years ago. Not so much a writing residency as a new institute bringing together writers, artists, thinkers, and academics from various parts of the world. I went there in September 2018, although it seems much more recent than that. The idea for the novel came to me while I was there, even though I had gone to write something else. I was working on a book about music, which eventually became Finding the Raga . Then I began, within a few days of being there, thinking of writing what is now Château Rouge . How this happens – the act of “writing” – is something I’ve written about before, including in my seventh novel, Friend of My Youth , and in a Paris Review column I wrote called “ The Moment .” What I point out there is that, for me, writing doesn't necessarily mean putting words on paper. Of course, I still write longhand, so literally, for me, it does involve writing words in a notebook. But writing doesn't necessarily begin at the moment when you start putting those words down.

For me, writing means a change in reality. It’s the moment when I enter a different kind of textual space, when I enter the act of writing and the transformation of meaning that writing involves. That doesn’t necessarily mean I’m thinking about writing anything down. It means that something has shifted in the reality I’m inhabiting: I begin to think about it differently and experience it differently. It no longer has only the everyday, unconscious dimensions of life; it also acquires the capacity to create connections and generate meanings specific to a particular kind of work.

Usually, when you say that you’ve written about something you’ve experienced, you imagine a sequential process: you experience something, and then you write about it, or you decide to write about it. For me, it isn’t sequential. Something shifts within that reality, and I begin to understand that this is now part of a text or a fiction – not in the sense that it is fictional, but in the sense that the demarcation between reality and representation no longer holds. There is an alteration in the way I understand what is around me.

I remember becoming aware of this for the first time when I was writing my third novel, Freedom Song . The Babri Masjid had come down, and it was winter. I was walking around Kolkata, in the area of South Kolkata where we live, and suddenly the BJP lotus painted on a wall looked different to me. The Babri Masjid, winter, the leaves that had fallen on the pavement, the BJP symbol on the wall, the differences between Hindus and Muslims, the eating of oranges, my retired father and my mother in that flat – all of these things suddenly began to come together in a way that they come together in a piece of writing. I knew that something had begun. I would now look at every detail through this connectedness, this textual connectedness, which gave everything a kind of freshness. But it wasn’t as if I was gathering experiences in order to write about them. Because my stories don't have conventional plots as such, it's very easy for me to confuse and conflate the everyday that is lived in with the everyday that is written about. Those demarcations don't hold; they spill into each other.

As far as this novel is concerned, the moment my wife said, just to calm me down, “This is where the writers would have lived. Hemingway would have lived here, not in some fancy made-up place,” I began to see everything around me differently. She said this because I had been thinking about vacating that flat which I had just arrived in in Paris that very evening, or the next day, given the state of disrepair it was in. The evening came and went, and the next morning I woke up intending to follow through on that impulse. But the moment she said that, my way of seeing the place changed. That alteration in seeing, for me, is writing. It doesn't matter whether it is written down or not. So I would say the writing began then. The actual writing, however, would have begun after I completed Sojourn , sometime in 2022.

I was really interested in that particular moment you referred to, when you say that the narrator brings into existence a kind of language by living in Château Rouge – a non-linguistic form of writing or language, as you say in the book. In fact, this novel seems to be constantly reckoning with the weight of history and with narratives that already exist within us and within particular spaces. There is, of course, the idea of Hemingway’s Paris, which the narrator is very eager to resist and rail against. I wanted to return to something you mentioned in your previous answer: that you don’t necessarily experience things knowing that you’re going to write about or narrate them. I find that distinction fascinating because I wonder how one does that. Does the knowledge that you might eventually narrate an experience not alter the experience itself? Once you begin to think of an experience as something you will have to gather, shape, and eventually transform into a narrative, does that change the way you experience it in the first place? That is precisely what doesn’t happen. I’m not collecting experience in order to create a narrative out of it in the future. I am extending the idea of narrative – I’ll use the word “narrative” sparingly – and extending the idea of writing and language. Language is not just the letters you type out or write down. It is a kind of change to the reality in which you exist; it is a field of possible meanings.

That field can exist within a work, but it isn’t confined to a work or to a particular piece of fiction. It can exist within it, but it can also exist continuously with it, outside it. It can exist between one book and another, between one book and a very different kind of book, or between one work and another work in a different genre. It can also be continuous with the actual here and now around me. The here and now need not be a foil or a background to the work, nor does it need to be its interior or its setting. It can be continuous with it.

The clearest way of seeing this in terms of a particular genre is the raga, which is why I bring up the raga in a particular section of Château Rouge . This mention of the raga in the book has partly to do with the laws of verisimilitude that are supposed to be obeyed while composing a novel (in this case, the man is in Paris ostensibly to write a book on music). I don’t set much store by those laws, though; I wouldn’t obey them if they had nothing to give me as a writer writing that kind of narrative. But the narrator is writing about music, so I bring the raga in for that reason. I also bring it in to comment on the remarks scattered throughout the text, and throughout some of my other texts, about how I relate to reality and how I think about writing.

This is something I’ve said in Finding the Raga : a raga has perhaps for the last 600 or 700 years been connected to something in the world – specifically, to a time of day or a season. Ragas are seasonal, or they are sung at particular times of day. Because of this, and because we tend to think about language and art in terms of representation – a way of thinking in which we’ve been schooled by the Enlightenment – we tend to assume that an afternoon raga must somehow be about the afternoon. There must be something in the raga that evokes the afternoon.

But, as I say in Finding the Raga , there is nothing in a raga’s notes that makes it more or less appropriate to a particular time of day. You can find other ragas with identical notes that are sung at completely different times of day or in different seasons. So an afternoon raga is not about the afternoon; it is of the afternoon. It is not about the world; it is of the world.

When you sing an afternoon raga, you do so because singing Madhuvanti would sound as wrong in the evening or at night as using the word “night” for “afternoon.” We are in a kind of interrelationship of words and reality. One thing is not outside the other, waiting to be represented. So one of the things that Madhuvanti comprises, besides its notes and its composition, is afternoon. You sing Madhuvanti – ni sa ga ma pa, pa ma ga re sa , and so on – and those notes are part of its text. The words of the composition are part of its text. But afternoon is also part of its text. This means that it is possible to understand the world as a field of meaning, rather than necessarily as something that needs to be meaningfully represented. In that sense, I think of fiction, and the novel, as one among a set of things that comprise language. And in that set is Château Rouge itself.

There is a paragraph in this novel where you refer to Sartre, and you discuss his idea that we become aware of being inside an adventure only when we begin to recount it. You then go on to suggest that we have become reliant on, and even hungry for, a rather turgid idea of history. I was curious about this idea of history that you seem to be reckoning with throughout the novel. There seems to be a kind of hollowed-out version of history that is both accessible and ever-present – the monuments and landmarks scattered throughout Paris, for instance, or the places associated with Hemingway and his fellow writers. But history also becomes inaccessible for precisely the same reason: because these places have already been so thoroughly marked and narrated as historical. I’m thinking, for instance, of the copy of A Moveable Feast that has been lying on the narrator’s nightstand. I was wondering if you could talk a little more about this idea of history, particularly about your resistance to the way history is made available to us through these pre-existing narratives and markers. Sartre, in Nausea , says that for something to become an adventure, it is necessary and sufficient to recount it. Something like that, in translation. What he means is that when you are in the midst of something, you don’t designate it as an adventure. You are busy trying to plug a leak, fix something, get somewhere after your car has broken down, or stop yourself from falling. You simply live through it. It is only later, when you describe it, that you call it an adventure: “I had an amazing adventure. Thank God I survived it,” or whatever it might be.

I’ve written about this in a short essay, where I suggest that the only time you can become aware that something is an adventure is when you undertake it for no outcome, or at least for no material outcome. I remember a time when my guitarist in England and I travelled to Edinburgh – or perhaps Glasgow, I can’t remember – to have me sing one of my songs on a BBC programme. The amount of money they were giving us would barely cover our travel expenses. My guitarist said, “Makes sense. It’s an adventure.” And that’s precisely because there was no treasure at the end, no material outcome. We undertook it enthusiastically, but for no particular purpose. In that sense, it could be experienced as an adventure. It is close to the idea of art as “purposefulness without a purpose”: an adventure, in my guitarist’s sense, is something undertaken without a predetermined outcome. Usually, though, what we call an adventure is a significant episode – something potentially life-changing, full of thrills or danger. And Sartre suggests that we recognise it as an adventure only in the recounting. I like this idea, and I think it may also belong to a broader French or Parisian way of thinking about the act of recounting.

Sartre’s Nausea is followed, chronologically, by Roland Barthes’s Writing Degree Zero , where Barthes refers to Paul Valéry’s observation that the novel always begins with a sentence such as “The Marquise went out at five o’clock.” That sentence immediately translates an event into a recounting. Barthes then says that this act of recounting in the past tense is the unreal time of novels, cosmogonies and histories. So he includes history within this idea of something that is always narrated. He calls narration or recounting an “unreal time” because it suppresses what he calls the trembling of existence – the unrecounted, the here and now.

In some ways, both Sartre and Barthes are drawing our attention to the transformation that takes place through narration, whether in the novel or in history. I came to believe, through speaking to people, that what Sartre says about the adventure is equally true of the historical. People don't know that they are living in history. They only know this if they are fictional characters in a certain kind of historical film, where they somehow understand that they are in the 17th century or in the middle of Partition and that this is history. My father lived through Partition. My parents were displaced by it. But they didn’t speak about Partition in a way that was fundamentally different from the way they spoke about the rest of their lives. They didn’t say, “This is history, whereas that was just my life.” They spoke about it as part of what was happening to them at that particular point in their lives. Other things happened at other points; this happened then. If my parents were fictional characters in a certain kind of novel, however, they would probably exude an awareness of the historicity of that moment. But they didn’t.

I have encountered the same thing in conversations about other supposedly historical moments. I once spoke to an Indian man, Kishore Bhimani, who had been in New York and had listened to John Coltrane. He had really enjoyed it. I asked him, “Did you know that you were in the middle of something historically significant?” He said, “No, I had no idea. We were just listening to him, and we thought this was great.” It’s only in the recounting that it becomes an adventure, that it becomes history. You have to begin with the sentence, “The Marquise went out at five o’clock.” You have to put it into the simple past tense. Otherwise, you don’t know.

This not-knowing is of great interest to me. It is also, I think, a rebuttal of historiography and of the way historiography is presented to us: taken out of the moment, transformed into something that can be identified as history. My preoccupation with the moment, and with the banal and the quotidian, is therefore also an angle from which I approach historiography. It is a way of questioning how we conceive of historical reality and how we invent an idea of history that can then foreclose so much of our experience.

If we subscribe to that idea of history, we cannot experience Château Rouge . We are chained to a particular Paris. We have to go around it again and again, and everything we encounter will simply confirm what we already know. It prevents us from experiencing anything else. It forecloses the hidden historicity – or what I would call the true historicity – that exists in the present, but has none of the markers of historicity that we recognise through monuments, famous buildings and other established sites. For Hemingway, for instance, there was no café that he could visit because it was “the café where Hemingway had hung out.” There was no such place for him. And for Gauguin and Van Gogh, there were no cafés where they could sit because Gauguin and Van Gogh had once been there. They lived in dreary places; they didn’t have much money, and they inhabited the here and now. They never tried to turn that moment into some kind of adventure in the past. You can see this in Van Gogh’s paintings of cafés and bedrooms. They don’t have the air of something already recounted. They remain in the now.

I’m really intrigued by the way you describe certain kinds of historiography as foreclosing the possibilities of experience, and by this idea of novel time. You have talked elsewhere about the possibilities offered by the unreal time of the novel, which nonfiction or memoir cannot necessarily offer; the form of the novel can sometimes enable a greater freedom in engaging with experience. I was thinking about this in relation to the narrator of Château Rouge , particularly the way the “I” moves so freely throughout the novel, and about how we have been referring to you, the author, and the narrator of the novel interchangeably all this time. I wanted to ask what the “I” means for you in Château Rouge . You do categorise the book as a novel, even though the form allows for such expansive movement between experience, memory, history and invention. How might we think about the “I” in this text? The “I” in the novel is, first of all, caught up in certain novelistic parameters. If I say, “I went out, I closed the door behind me, I went into the room, it was hot, I was absorbed by what I saw,” the narrative parameters immediately come into play. The syntax of narrative fiction comes into play even as one is dismantling it. That tension is very interesting to me as a writer because it gives me the opportunity to take those parameters on directly – to embrace them in order to dismantle them, and in order to do something new with them – rather than rejecting them and writing in a completely different genre, such as the essay, which I also write.

The moment I write an essay, the “I” becomes somewhat different. It isn’t doing all the things that the “I”, or any character, has to do within a work of fiction: performing actions that are narrated in a particular way and in sequence. The “I” in an essay can simply remain an “I”, a voice. You don’t have to enact yourself in an essay. You can, of course, but it would be odd for an essay to be full of statements like, “I went and opened a window.” Why would you say that in an essay? That is a particular kind of narrative tic, and a very necessary one.

For me, it is important to embrace this seemingly boring part of fiction writing in order to play with all kinds of other meanings that would not be available to me in an essay. In an essay, that particular tension would begin to disappear, and I would simply be narrating something. I love the essay as a form, but the “I”, and the idea of characterisation that pertains to it, would remain much more placid than it does in what we call a novel.

Here, the “I” is performing these actions, or non-actions, while also being subjected to a kind of scrutiny by the narrator, by the imagination at work. That scrutiny reveals that this “I” is the kind of person who claims, perhaps quite honestly, to dislike the idea of a writer’s Paris – to dislike Proust’s Paris, Baldwin’s Paris, Hemingway’s Paris. But the moment the opportunity to have anything to do with that Paris, even to deride it, is taken away from him, he begins to panic. He wants at least to be in that Paris which he recognises as Paris, so that he can then reject it. He wants to be unhappy in that Paris – the Paris of the canon, of convention. He wants that, and he is completely at sea in this unknown terrain, which doesn’t seem to be Paris at all. And this isn’t because he has ever wanted to be in Proust’s Paris or to make a pilgrimage to Proust’s house. It is simply because he doesn’t know how to live a life that isn’t about not fitting into the centre of things.

In Château Rouge , he has been left behind. There is no question of not fitting into the centre of things because he isn’t anywhere near the centre. He doesn’t know how to deal with this until his wife suddenly opens up other possibilities for him: the possibility of looking at this particular place as Paris itself.

In your essay, “ First Sentence ,” in Granta , you talk about how storylines fatigue you, and how distraction can, in fact, be productive for you. You also describe writing in terms of the paragraph as a unit, rather than thinking of the novel as a whole. That seems to be particularly evident in Château Rouge , with its brisk, nonlinear fragments that continually move between different thoughts and moments. For me, those fragments created a remarkable sense of immediacy. I remember one instance where you realise, within the very sentence in which you are describing a street, that you have got its name wrong, and you correct yourself in real time. I was interested in what this kind of writing assumes about the reader. Do you have a reader or a kind of reading practice in mind when you write? I suppose the simple answer is that I don’t have any reader in mind. I have the work in mind. I’m thinking about the work and what it is I’m trying to do. When I revise, I’m thinking about how to make it readable to myself, especially because, after I’ve written something, parts of it – or sometimes quite a lot of it – can seem bad, inert or dead. I have to deal with that problem. There is no simple fix for making a piece of writing come alive. It’s something you have to seek out as you work and rework the piece. Sometimes you think that life is impossible to reach, and then you take out a word or change something slightly, and suddenly it’s there. No matter how interesting the material is, or how meaningful it is to you, there is absolutely no guarantee that it will be alive as a piece of writing. That is primarily what I’m trying to figure out.

In doing that, of course, I am both the writer and the reader, just as the singer and the listener are two discrete but related entities. They exist together, separate but also enmeshed in one another. But to say simply that the reader is me makes it sound oddly reductive. The reader is the part of me that notices things, remembers things and assigns value to certain things that may not necessarily seem valuable to the other me that is also moving through the world.

It’s risky to try to pin this down to a pronoun, but that reader is certainly at work when you’re writing. As far as writing in the way I do is concerned, this is something that has been happening since my first novel, A Strange and Sublime Address : the nightmare of deleting paragraphs, putting new ones in, and making something like a narrative seem to come into existence through paragraphs that didn’t originally follow one another. All of that has been happening from the beginning. Because this process doesn’t quite resemble the way a novel is conventionally supposed to be written, I’ve been forced to think about it. But it is also an exploration of how one might write, and of what one can get away with, in order to pursue this preoccupation with what you call immediacy, as well as the other preoccupations we've been discussing. How do you make that happen? How do you make it stand up?

Every writer is, in some sense, exploring a way of making this happen anew. There is no predetermined path, definition or process for it. That doesn’t mean, of course, that we aren’t in conversation with other writers and their work. There is certainly a community of writers, extending from the past into the present, whose ways of thinking may be more congenial to me than others. But the process remains extremely murky. It’s complicated and life-consuming. I think you spend your life consumed by this conundrum: what you’re doing, why you’re doing it, and why you’re doing it in that particular way. There is barely time to think about anything else. It’s a life of bewilderment, some pleasure, disappointment and disconnection from the world, and yet also a renewed connection with the world through what it is you do and why you do it. And that continues over years and years. That’s the way it is.

Since you’ve been talking about the writer’s responsibility to the work they are creating, I can’t help but ask about the writer’s relationship with the present. Do you think a writer has a responsibility to the present in what they write – to capture something about the particular moment in which they are living, or to respond to the realities around them? Should the writer bear this burden of capturing or bearing witness to the present in a certain way, or do you think of the writer as ultimately free from that burden? I’m trying to think about what the word “responsibility” might mean here. If it means a conventional, citizenly idea of responsibility, then I’m not sure the writer has that responsibility in the act of writing. They might be responsible citizens in other ways, in the way they lead their lives. But when they are writing, the mind is un-citizenly. The act of writing is un-citizenly, and it is valuable for it to be that way. Otherwise, a kind of suffocation takes place.

When the right to indifference is taken away from us, we also lose the kind of indifference that can create value. I think the primary attachment a writer, or even a thinker, has is to explore that domain of freedom which verges on the irresponsible, the indifferent, the absurd. Without these dimensions, our constitutional freedoms begin to become hollow. We should all have the right to bring down our sacred deities – not only through acts of satire or pointed irreverence, but through truly disruptive indifference. Someone should have the right, at some point, to say something completely disrespectful of whatever it is that is most sacred to us, whether that sacredness is constitutional or religious. So it’s not an either–or. The religious, the non-religious, the constitutional – all of these should be open to being ignored as the great verities that guide our lives. That has historically been important in creating the domain of freedom. We are not shackled to one idea of freedom or another, or to one idea of the self or another.

This is where I think the writer’s negotiation of these questions becomes not only important but risky. It requires a great deal of cleverness and intelligence – something that the writer can bring to it. I don’t think writers are bringing much intelligence to this at the moment. They have in the past; theorists and thinkers have as well. But right now, everything seems extremely black and white. It requires a great deal of intelligence to negotiate this particular journey between citizenliness and un-citizenliness, in life and in the present climate, just as it has in any climate in the past. That is something writers can do, but they can do it only if they are courageous and bring all their powers of reflection and intellect to what they are doing.

That is remarkably put. So, as we’ve discussed, all across Château Rouge, you dance around the possibility of reading a certain novel by Hemingway. That brings us to my final question: did you enjoy finally reading A Moveable Feast ? It’s a wonderful book. It’s become one of my favourite things by Hemingway. As I said in the novel, I had always avoided Hemingway. There are a few things of his that I really liked, including some short stories and a longer story called Big Two-Hearted River , but those were few and far between. Now A Moveable Feast is definitely not only one of my favourite Hemingway books, but one of my favourite books in general. I’m glad that I finally got around to reading it. But it was also a gift that the whole idea of reading and living came together in the book. You lived your life, and there was a moment when you would be reading. I wasn't consciously thinking about this while writing, but it was only later that I began to realise that my wife must have made that comment because she had read A Moveable Feast . Then I began to think about the book itself, and the fact that I hadn’t read it. That became part of the thought and structure of the novel: the fact of not having read the book, what that book is, and the fact that I would eventually read it. So, yes, that was a wonderful experience.

editorials.title: How AI could influence our understanding of mathematics: A computer scientist-novelist’s reflections
editorials.passage:
On September 8, OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes problem. “The question of whether smooth three-dimensional fluid motion can break down has remained unresolved for roughly 90 years,” Open AI said. It put 10,000 AI agents to work on it and the task took 88 hours. What might this mean for how we “do” mathematics?

It is not really clear how mathematicians chose to become mathematicians. After all, there are no “creative mathematics” courses for the budding mathematician the way there are “creative writing” courses for the budding storyteller or poet. There are no celebrity mathematicians to crush on (let’s ignore Brian Cox). Mathematics books for children have ominous reassurances of just how fun , just how easy , just how natural the subject is; this is in direct contradiction with the student’s own experience. So either the books are lying or the student is a duffer. Frankly, given the circumstances, it is a wonder anyone becomes a mathematician.

Though we do not know how mathematicians are made, we do know what mathematicians do after they become professional mathematicians. They work on proofs. That’s really it. They prove things day in and day out, and if they have time left to spare or if their lunch money depends on it, then they’ll indoctrinate hapless graduate students to also prove things day in and day out. If this life seems charmless, that’s because it is. Until, of course, one proves a result so spectacular, so beautiful, so difficult, one can have it engraved on your butt. That moment makes it worth all the years of tears and salt.

Such a result was achieved on September 8 when a long-standing question about the Navier-Stokes equation was finally settled by two teams. One team was composed of AI agents and the other by a couple of human mathematicians who made use of AI tech. They showed – meaning, they proved – that the Navier-Stokes equation can exhibit singularities.

The details of the achievement don’t particularly matter here. The Navier-Stokes equation describes the behaviour of a class of liquids. Since liquids misbehave in all conceivable ways, it is a gnarly beast. Claude-Louis Navier, who first formulated the equation in 1822, almost failed his École Polytechnique entrance exams. He also built a bridge that collapsed from the weight of all the assumptions he’d piled on the design.

On the other hand, George Stokes, who provided the first reasonably rigorous derivation of the equation in 1845, was already getting cow-eyed by Oxbridge when he made Senior Wrangler in the notoriously difficult Mathematical Tripos exams.

How did Claude-Louis Navier and George Stokes get interested in math? Claude-Louis Navier, I suspect, could just as easily have been diverted to write theses on literary criticism. Stokes’s interest in waves, in all the wonderful weirdness of liquids, seems to have originated in the idyllic childhood spent living very close to the Atlantic Ocean. His home was a mere 3.5 km from Dunmoran Strand beach in Skreen, Ireland. This makes for a nice story, but plenty of us live very close to garbage dumps and yet somehow fail to take an interest in the mathematics of garbage. All we can really say is that living close to the beach didn’t subtract from George Stokes’s mathematical inclinations.

What if we have our kids living, not near the ocean, but adjacent to a friendly AI? When they have a problem with fractions, the AI is there to help out. If it’s help with a doctoral thesis, why not? The AI is there to help with that too. At every step, the AI surrounds our young, nudging them, guiding them, infinitely patient, infinitely competent, and infinitely forgiving. Would kids still choose to become mathematicians? Or would they never get over their awe of their first and last teacher, the AI, and settle for viewing mathematics as a spectator sport?

It’s tempting to argue that just as chess programs didn’t kill off human interest in chess, AI won’t kill off human interest in mathematics. The difference is this: any game of chess is independent of every other game of chess. So you can isolate games humans play with other humans from the games humans play with programs. Segregation brings with the illusion that some sort of parity has been achieved.

That is not the case with mathematics. You cannot solve a problem in mathematics without it influencing other solutions. Humans cannot isolate the mathematics problems they solve from the problems an AI solves. For example, the fact that the two teams cracked the singularity problem means that going forward, mathematicians must accept that this result exists. If AI can “do” mathematics, then clearly, the way we do mathematics has to change.

What does it mean to “do” mathematics? It is not, as OTT shows like Prime Target would have you believe, to be good-looking and have the ability to see π everywhere. Doing mathematics has come to indicate one very specific talent: the ability to prove things.

Proofs have become the skeleton, bones, flesh and lifeblood of mathematics. Once a student leaves high school, they enter the world of mathematical proofs. Every claim they encounter in a math textbook has a proof. To know something in math is to have a proof for it. In fancy terms, knowledge is valid inference.

It is this bedrock that will need to be rethought. AI will soon, if it is not already, become far better at developing proofs than humans. In fact, we will come to see that the miracle isn’t that machines can do proofs; it is that we are so good at it. What is left for humans to do?

Plenty. The fact that we can outsource much of proof development to programs is one of the best things that could have happened to mathematics. Proofs have been getting impossibly unwieldy. As our mathematical problems get ever subtler, the landscape has gotten increasingly treacherous. We need a vehicle to help us fly over it and not have to trudge for years on end through thicket and turbulence. AI is that vehicle.

For the past 200 years or so, mathematics has selected for a certain kind of mind: detail-oriented, obsessive, narrow-focused and immune to boredom. It is as if poetry were practised by only allowing poets with a passion for prosody. This move towards turning proof into a near-fetish object isn’t accidental. Nor was it unjustified. A great many mistakes were made by 17th- and 18th-century mathematicians because they didn’t understand the importance of rigour.

It is just that in achieving rigour, through magisterial projects like those of David Hilbert or the Bourbaki school, mathematics became afraid of speculation and play. Mathematics books are devoid of humour, personality and any indication that a human mind contemplated the results. The texts are an endless succession of claims, proofs and exercises. The student is warned that to miss the exercises is to ensure failure as a mathematician. Definitions are unmotivated, history is almost always ignored, and alternate theoretical approaches, failed or otherwise, are rarely discussed. In the more abstract areas, any application to “real-world” problems is viewed with some dismay.

It’s no use to appeal to one’s professors because they reveal only the survivor’s lack of compassion. As the broken scholar, now a tenured academic, approaches the twilight of their mediocrity, a certain frivolity is permitted: a note on the golden ratio in the local newspaper, some twaddle on the importance of intuition in creativity, or perhaps even – this is pushing their luck with the department chair – the need to reform the system.

But there is another kind of mathematics and another kind of mathematician. This style is embodied by mathematicians like Leonhard Euler, Srinivasa Ramanujan and John Horton Conway, René Thom and the sparkling imaginativeness of their work. René Thom, a Fields Medallist, is especially interesting. Ivar Ekeland, in his obituary essay on Thom, wrote:

“When I first met René Thom, in 1970, he was already a legend in mathematics. There were many stories about him, which were reverently passed around. It was said, for instance, that his thesis adviser, back in the early 1950s, was concerned that he could not get Thom to write satisfactory mathematical proofs; another eminent mathematician told the adviser not to worry– there are ten people in the world, he said, who can prove these theorems once they have been stated, but only Thom can state them.

“Indeed, Thom's own lectures gave some credence to such tales. He was a geometrician; he saw things in his mind and would try to impart his vision with all the means at his disposal, whether they were pictures on the blackboard or analogies from other sciences. In French mathematics, he was unique in this respect. There was general agreement at the time that serious mathematicians were in the business of devising proofs, not explaining them. The meaning of a theorem should be worked out from its formal proof. With Thom, it was the other way around. He showed why things were true, or should be true, and left his audience to work out the proofs.”

Perhaps this is the kind of mind which the new age of mathematics will favour. A mind which delights in speculation, leaps of the imagination, a deep sense of aesthetics, and a personal style which can even imprint how a field gets to be studied. It is mathematics approached as play. The philosopher Bernard Suits wrote that “playing a game is the voluntary attempt to overcome unnecessary obstacles.”

It is precisely this voluntary acceptance of the lack of necessity which turns mathematics into art, and the kind of art which brings with it the joys of play. No doubt the day will surely come when the universe will see fit, just as it did with us, to turn to these engines of our devising to answer its own enigma, but for now, the responsibility of asking the right kind of wrong questions remains our prerogative.

Anil Menon is a computer scientist and a fiction writer. His most recent work is the novel The Coincidence Plot. It was preceded by a collection of his speculative short fiction, The Inconceivable Idea Of The Sun: Stories. He is currently the chief editor of The Bombay Literary Magazine.

editorials.title: Ramachandra Guha: India needs fearless civil liberties activists more than ever
editorials.passage:
I work mostly by myself, and have resisted joining alumni associations and WhatsApp groups. I am, in other words, broadly of the same mind as Groucho Marx, who famously said that he would never join a club which would have him as a member.

Yet for a few brief years in Delhi in the 1980s, I associated myself with the People’s Union for Democratic Rights, a citizens group that sought to hold the Indian State to account for the varied crimes it committed against Indian citizens. I attended the PUDR’s Saturday meetings at the Triveni Kala Sangam, paid a very modest amount from my stipend to help fund its reports, and on one occasion even joined a fact-finding group it had organised.

I was never a core member of PUDR, merely a fellow traveller, a sympathiser hovering around its outer circle. However, I admired the organisation and its work enormously, and thus felt a certain kinship with it, which was lost when I left Delhi for Bangalore in the early 1990s. Memories of what the PUDR had once meant to me came back while reading Ankita Pandey’s recently published book, Becoming Allies: Civil Liberties Activism in India .

Pandey views civil liberties groups as an illustration of what she calls “ally activism”, defined as “collective action undertaken in solidarity with a marginalized group by those who do not have a direct, personal or material stake in the cause”. As she observes, there have been two broad trends in the civil liberties movement in India; one that focuses on safeguarding the rights of citizens as codified in the Constitution, a second that canvasses for broader social and economic rights.

By all accounts, the oldest civil liberties group in independent India is the Calcutta-based Association for Protection of Democratic Rights, which took shape in the early 1970s. Among its early campaigns was to urge the humane treatment in prison of those associated with the Naxalite movement. The prisoners themselves had launched a bidi-chiththi andolan , demanding access to cigarettes and letters from friends and family. The APDR then amplified these demands to include better food and living conditions, and also the release of the prisoners themselves.

If the APDR was chronologically the first of these groups, then perhaps the most wide-ranging in its work has been the PUDR. Over the decades, the PUDR has published close to 300 reports, documenting such issues as police brutality against undertrials, encounter deaths, the precarious condition of unorganised labour, laws dispossessing tribals of rights to forests and other natural resources, crimes against women, violence against Dalits, and state discrimination against religious minorities. Many (though not all) of these reports are available on the PUDR website.

Other important human rights groups in India include the People’s Union for Civil Liberties, headquartered in Delhi but with branches in several states, and whose prime mover was the jurist, VM Tarkunde; the Andhra Pradesh Civil Liberties Committee; the Human Rights Forum, also active in Andhra Pradesh; and the Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, which operates largely in Maharashtra, and one of whose founders was the social activist, Asghar Ali Engineer.

A key chapter in Pandey’s book focuses on the fact-finding reports that are “the predominant mode of activism for civil liberties groups in India”. These reports seek to document the culpability of the State and State officials in fuelling violence and thereby violating the safety, security, and democratic rights of citizens.

They are based on the findings of individuals deputed to conduct an on-the-spot investigation of the events concerned.

Pandey argues that these fact-finding reports have served three key functions. First, they “transformed people’s recollections into legally helpful artefacts. The teams systematised, verified and documented testimonies in a form that would render them acceptable to a judicial commission or a court”. Second, these reports contained “a detailed description of the context and history to counter the technical and depersonalised official records of the same events”. And “the third element in the practice of fact-finding was locating gaps, outlining inconsistencies and exposing fudged records within the police and administrative documentation and reports.”

In sum, these fact-finding reports have aimed “to contradict, expose and highlight the inconsistencies in the official narratives in order to question their credibility in the eyes of the press and the public. They brought governmental wrongdoing to the spotlight and exposed the biases and prejudices of state functionaries”.

These civil liberties groups are entirely volunteer-driven, sustained by the work of individuals committed to their cause. They do not take foreign or corporate funds and tirelessly labour on in the face of societal prejudice and state hostility. Apart from the external pressures on their functioning, they also face an internal challenge; namely, to demonstrate that, while being critical of the State, they are at the same time independent of all political parties.

A second internal challenge these groups have had to confront is the question of gender justice. Some of the leading activists of groups like PUDR and the APCLC were women. However, their male colleagues thought the focus should be exclusively on the public violence committed by the state against citizens, arguing that violence within the domain of the family or the household should not be their concern.

This was questioned by the female activists, who pointed out, for example, that in several parts of India the number of dowry deaths exceeded the number of custodial deaths. Eventually, these groups came to acknowledge that women’s rights were indeed a key part of a broader framework of democratic rights and incorporated this element in their work.

In Becoming Allies , Ankita Pandey notes that those active in civil liberties groups are disproportionately drawn from three professions; academics, journalism and the law. These members of the salaried middle-class are animated by a spirit of sacrifice and idealism, seeking to make India a more just and humane society. Their character is often marked by self-effacement, downplaying their own role.

Pandey quotes the activist lawyer, Sudha Bharadwaj, the daughter of two eminent academics and herself a graduate of the prestigious Indian Institute of Technology at Kanpur, as saying about her incarceration by the Indian state: “No doubt three years in jail has been painful, but there are many people more unfortunate than me. My heart went out to them. When you are in the midst of so much misery, it is difficult to be miserable for oneself; you have to help others.”

This self-effacement was also characteristic of the late CV Subba Rao, for many years the moving spirit of the PUDR. He goes unmentioned in Becoming Allies , even though the book starts with Who are the Guilty , the landmark report on the anti-Sikh riots of 1984. Subba Rao played a key role in the writing of this report, as in giving shape to the work of the PUDR more broadly. His absence from Pandey’s narrative is not be held against her, for it is merely a mark of how the man himself refused ever to take any credit for the work he did for others. One had to meet and observe Subba Rao in flesh and blood to know him for what he really was, namely, a true hero of Indian democracy.

Such omissions notwithstanding, Ankita Pandey’s Becoming Allies provides a valuable overview of the civil liberties movement as a whole and may be read in conjunction with the late Nilanjan Dutta’s Civil Liberties Movement in India: From Colonial Times to the Present .

These books are particularly timely in the present context, when democratically-minded citizens face multiple threats – from, among other things, the apathy of the media, the brutality of the police, the indifference of the courts, and the active opposition of the Narendra Modi regime.

In light of a creeping authoritarianism and a galloping majoritarianism, India now needs civil liberties activists more than ever.

This article first appeared in The Telegraph.

editorials.title: ‘White Elephant’: Jeyamohan’s excellent novel is backed by an equally excellent translation
editorials.passage:
On Chennai’s Kamaraja Salai, just off Marina Beach, stands a large circular building now known as Vivekanandar Illam, after Swami Vivekananda, who stayed here for a while. It’s a city landmark, but relatively few people know of the building’s blood-soaked past, its connections to Chennai’s colonial history as well as to caste politics, commercialism – and the sheer ruthlessness and greed of those who would not let anything come in the way of their ambition for power and wealth. Till 1880, this edifice was the Ice House at Madras, built in 1842 by American merchant-businessman Frederic Tudor to store ice shipped from the lakes and ponds of New England.

Jeyamohan’s Vellai Yaani , translated from the Tamil into English by Priyamvada Ramkumar as White Elephant , has the Ice House as the pivotal setting of the novel. It is here that the protagonist, Captain Aiden Byrne, first sees the 30-tonne block of ice that ends up changing his life and his way of thinking. The edges had thawed and blunted, turning it into a bevelled square. A square elephant. A white elephant. It is 1876, and the ruthless exploitation of Dalit workers allows the Ice House to function. Outside Madras, a famine rages through the Deccan and other parts of India: thousands are starving, but Aiden, the Irishman serving in Her Majesty’s army, does not realise the magnitude or the horror of the famine until a chance encounter brings him face to face with the truth.

One day, riding through town, Aiden sees an overseer from the Ice House thrashing two people: a worker at the Ice House and his wife. Aiden is horrified, and his sense of outrage mounts when he visits the Ice House, sees conditions there, and in turn receives a visit from Kathavarayan, an educated, charismatic Dalit activist. Kathavarayan is the catalyst for Aiden to explore the Dalit community’s settlement in Madras, and to drive into the ravaged countryside, towards Chingleput, where the famine is at its worst. To stand up to injustice, even against overwhelming odds.

The Dalit labour protest at the Ice House was not a well-documented episode, yet Jeyamohan brings it to life vividly, just as realistically as he depicts the horrors of the famine. Aiden’s harrowing journey towards Chingleput is the sort of literary passage that can sear itself into a reader’s mind, its harshness balanced with poignancy: the plight of these people is heart-rending, yet it is not just sorrow one feels, but anger too, because this was a man-made famine. And there are people around for whom making a tidy profit out of the deaths of countless others – because they are “untouchables” – is perfectly acceptable.

It would have been natural to make the protagonist of this story an Indian, one born and brought up in the milieu and therefore able to understand its nuances. By choosing to make an Irishman the focal character, Jeyamohan gives his novel further depth: for Aiden, his unfamiliarity with the caste system and with the socio-economic ramifications of profit, loss, exclusion and oppression becomes a matter of life and death. As his eyes are opened, so too are those of the reader. His rising anger at the status quo, and his sense of helplessness convey themselves more forcefully to the reader than might have been the case had the protagonist been, say, Kathavarayan.

While Aiden the British Army officer struggles to make a difference, there is, too, Aiden the Irishman: the man who has left his family behind in the Irish countryside years ago. The man who is painfully aware that the British have oppressed his people in ways very similar to how they treat Indians. The mounting turmoil, the sense of being torn between Ireland and Britain, between those he serves and those he sees as similar to his own people: Jeyamohan depicts Aiden with a sensitivity and candour that is very real.

This nuanced depiction carries forward into other areas too. If Aiden is horrified at how the Brahmins treat the Dalits, why does he not feel the same sense of horror at using a man’s back as a step when alighting from his carriage? Why, through much of the story, does he not realise that his lover, the Anglo-Indian woman Marisa, is in a similar situation as the people he feels so sorry for? Why is Captain Byrne often bereft of the Irishman Aiden?

White Elephant is that rare book where every element – the characterisation, the story, the language, the emotion – is pitch-perfect. Aiden’s constant seeking of solace in the poetry of Shelley; the turbulence both within and without the man; the plight of the Dalits… this is a book which balances the macro with the micro, the individual with the structure he is part of, his nature and what he must mould it into, with a hard-hitting, gripping masterfulness that makes this one of the best Indian works of historical fiction to be translated into English in recent years.

Due credit must go to Priyamvada Ramkumar for an accomplished translation. Her choices are such that it never seems as if these words are anything but those of an Englishman (or an Irishman who has succeeded in moulding himself into a believable likeness of an Englishman). The cadence of the language, the way Ramkumar leaves some words – even, in one turbulent scene, entire sentences – in Tamil, the careful attention to words, make this a translation that does justice to the excellence of the original novel. Through most of White Elephant , it is easy to forget that this impactful language, with its lyricism and its sometimes made-up but so precise words, is not that of Jeyamohan himself. Take for example: “Through the black roads of hell. No. Through the gut of a mire-dwelling, malodorous beast. Gutways. Gutspirals. Gutwaste.”

Jeyamohan’s novel, in Ramkumar’s translation, makes for an absorbing, unsettling read. A fine example of skilled storytelling, and of equally skilled translation to back it up.

White Elephant: A Novel, Jeyamohan, translated from the Tamil by Priyamvada Ramkumar, HarperCollins India.

editorials.title: The US is playing favourites with its ‘America First’ Policy
editorials.passage:
In West Asia, recent developments are nearly unbelievable. First, the Houthis, once a ragtag force with possibly not even access to a decent phone, are now sending guided missiles and drones into Saudi Arabia, effectively closing the Bab al-Mandab, the main  shipping route through which roughly 10 to 12 per cent of global trade and around 30 per cent of global container traffic passes. That doesn’t seem to bother the United States. First, it made a deal with the Houthi leaders not to target US ships. Second, its House of Representatives passed legislation authorising tariffs up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian and Iranian oil or gas. Nice. Apparently everyone is supposed to just starve to death as energy prices climb. It’s beyond outrageous. But it’s not quite quixotic as one would suppose. Look closer.
Deal-making with the Houthis
First, the Houthi menace. The Houthi-Saudi Conflict has been going on for years, with Riyadh launching air attacks on them when they began taking over the Yemeni capital and threatened Saudi territory. This escalated sharply until a truce was declared in 2022, which collapsed as the Iran-Israel-US war escalated and the US and the UK came into the fight in 2024 in defence of Israel. Consider that by this time, the Houthis had amassed not just sophisticated weapons but also a clutch of long-range missiles, that included one that hit Israel’s Ben Gurion airport, some 2,000 km away. That says something not just about Houthi growing capability but also about the extent of Iranian help. The Houthis are not an outright Iranian tool. Earlier, they agreed to a ceasefire with the US, with Oman mediating an end to attacks on US ships. They, however, retained their right to attack Israel in support of the Palestinian cause. In other words, the US fended for itself and let its ally Israel take the heat quite literally.  Recently, US officials flatly refused to also defend Saudi Arabia, even while they met with Houthi leaders who assured them that the ceasefire stood. All this despite the fact that in 2025, the US designated them as a terrorist entity, noting that they had hit more than 100 ships. And this is what the order says, “It is the policy of the United States to cooperate with its regional partners to eliminate Ansar Allah’s capabilities and operations, deprive it of resources, and thereby end its attacks on U.S. personnel and civilians, U.S. partners, and maritime shipping in the Red Sea” (italics mine). That last bit has clearly been set aside. As the Houthis occupy Perim and other strategic islands on the Bab al-Mandab, global energy markets and shipping have taken a hit, and major shipping companies have moved to the longer, more expensive route around the Horn of Africa. Meanwhile, here’s the killer. The Trump administration is pushing US firms to rebuild damaged infrastructure in the West Asia, which would be worth billions, even as  US officials are looking at a trade-off where Gulf states use a currency swap line from the US firms for rebuilding. So it’s  America first and the devil take the hindmost.
US legislation: What it disallows — and allows
As the International Monetary Fund further reduced its growth forecasts for the global economy, the existing oil shock, and the  El Niño effect — which could push about 50 million people into acute hunger — are adding to the pressure. Government deficits have reached record highs in countries such as South Korea and Vietnam. India has so far managed to keep its deficit under control, but faces strong pressures in keeping food and fertiliser prices stable and sustaining its safety net schemes. It’s a tough call. It could get worse. As diesel dries up in the US, Trump could decide to cut exports. And its at this intersection of multiple crises  that the US House of Representatives chose to pass legislation authorising the President to impose tariffs up to 100 per cent on countries importing Russian oil or gas. Hang on though. That’s not all. There are ‘exceptions’ to this which include ‘activities carried out under an agreement for cooperation between the United States and the Russian Federation entered into under section 123 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and  Exception For Certain Imports Of Low-Enriched Uranium For Nuclear Reactors or medical isotopes for which a waiver has been issued..’ In short, uranium buys by the US don’t impede Russia’s war-waging capability, but oil imports by India or China do.
The problem for India
China doesn't care much. It still has a pipeline to rely on, and is already beginning to reduce its overall imports. As the denial of Iranian oil continues, official sources had said earlier that  India has ‘diversified’ its purchases. That  list includes UAE, Saudi Arabia and Russia. Over half of our imports still come from Russia, while the other two are still struggling to get their energy production back to normal.  For India, this whole thing is critical. And into this comes the official statements that the US accounts for 67 per cent of India’s LPG imports. Remember that India is the second-largest importer of LPG in the world. That marks a significant shift. Now add to that the fact that crude oil imports from Venezuela have climbed to a six-year high, which is also ‘managed’ by the US. Add to that the earlier promise that India would buy $500 billion worth of energy from the US as part of a trade deal. Add all this up and one can only conclude this is again America first, this time in terms of India’s energy basket. Down the road are other energy sources like Small Modular Reactors. In other words, more mathematical analysis shows not just a bid to supplant all others in supplying energy, but also a foreign policy that is hugely skewed not just in terms of American interests – which was always there, but suitably cloaked – but one that shows scant regard for development and financial realities on the ground.
The MEA takes umbrage
This is why the reaction of the Ministry of External Affairs has been unusually harsh. The MEA firmly notes its commitment to ‘ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people’ through ‘diversified sourcing’ noting its potential implications for the bilateral relationship. In diplomatese, that’s strong stuff.  And the critical part is: ‘The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests.’ That seems to point to a certain resistance to arm-twisting. The UAE, once a major supplier, has already begun to expand its ports and infrastructure on the eastern coast away from the Hormuz. Talks with Iran during the recent Brics summit in Delhi seem promising. Iran itself still offers the Chabahar port, which is capable of providing the cheapest route for crude. If India decides to opt for this source, it could form part of a broader mediation exercise focused on the aspect of the conflict most crucial to India: preserving peace between UAE and Iran. The Houthi war is Riyadh’s — and Pakistan’s — arena, as is the Iran-US war, which is Washington’s. Time to draw lines, not only on the map, but also in foreign policy. To do him justice, President Trump was never in favour of such huge tariff as those being proposed by the House. A small walkway is needed to get this through, together with some very tough diplomacy.

(The writer is a former Director, National Security Council Secretariat. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: India’s road to 2036 Olympics begins in schools
editorials.passage:
Somewhere in an Indian school today, a child is running faster than everyone else in her class. Nobody is timing her.

Another can play for hours without tiring. Someone else has exceptional balance, reflexes or hand-eye coordination. There may be a natural rower who has never seen a rowing boat, a weightlifter who has never lifted a barbell, or a shooter who has never held a rifle.

They are not athletes. Not yet. They are simply children carrying abilities that nobody has measured. And therein lies both the challenge and the opportunity for Indian sport.

For generations, we have largely discovered sporting talent after it has become visible. A child begins playing cricket, hockey, wrestling or athletics; performs well; someone notices; and the better ones gradually move up the system. It has produced champions. But it also leaves us with a fundamental question: what happens to the child who has extraordinary physical ability but never encounters the sport suited to that ability?

In a country of 1.4 billion people, that cannot be a small question. Perhaps we have been beginning the search one step too late. Instead of only asking children, “Which sport do you play?”, we should also be capable of discovering what their bodies are naturally capable of doing well. Speed. Strength. Endurance. Agility. Flexibility. Balance. Coordination.

Measure these scientifically and something interesting begins to happen. We are no longer only looking for athletes. We are discovering physical talent.

That distinction can change Indian sport. But I believe it can do something even bigger. India does not only need more Olympic champions. India needs a fitter generation. And fitness improves when it becomes visible. What gets measured gets noticed. A child who knows that her endurance has improved begins to understand fitness differently. A parent who can see changes in strength or flexibility begins to take physical development more seriously. A school that measures fitness begins to value it alongside other aspects of a child’s development.

So, the same system that searches for exceptional talent can create awareness of fitness among millions of ordinary children. That is why talent identification should not be imagined as an exercise to separate a few future Olympians from everybody else.

The first dividend is fitness for millions. The second is discovering excellence among them. And this is where India’s population can become a genuine sporting advantage. We often speak of 1.4 billion Indians as evidence of our enormous sporting potential. But population by itself is not potential. Population becomes potential only when ability can be identified, nurtured and connected to opportunity. Technology and sports science now allow us to attempt this at a scale that was impossible earlier.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call from the Red Fort to identify sporting talent among children between five and fifteen years of age therefore comes at an important moment. Consider the arithmetic. A five-year-old today will be fifteen in 2036. A ten-year-old will be twenty. A fifteen-year-old will be twenty-five. The generation that could represent India in 2036 is already here.

India has also spent the last decade building much of the sporting architecture required to support that generation: Khelo India at the grassroots, KIRTI for talent identification, the Target Olympic Podium Scheme at the elite level, and now the National Sports Policy 2025 with its emphasis on sports science, technology and modern coaching. The opportunity now is to connect the dots.
Measure. Discover. Track. Guide. Train. Compete. Excel.

Rajasthan, for instance, aligned with the Prime Minister’s vision, has begun exploring this through the PRATIBHA pilot. At PM SHRI Kendriya Vidyalaya No. 2 in Jaipur, 1,117 students underwent scientific physical assessments. The numbers themselves are not the most interesting part. What happens next is.

A sprint tells us something about a child today. An endurance test tells us something else. Strength, flexibility, agility and coordination add more pieces. But children grow differently. One child develops early; another at fourteen. Nutrition changes. Confidence changes. Training changes the body. So a single test can never become a judgement on a child. A snapshot can miss talent. A trajectory can reveal it.

Assess children periodically and those scattered numbers begin to form a story. We can see who is improving unusually quickly, where particular abilities are emerging and eventually, which sporting opportunities might suit that child. Then talent discovery is no longer dependent entirely on chance. And geography begins to matter less.

Why should a gifted rower only be discovered near a rowing centre? Why should a future cyclist have to be born near a cycling academy? Why should a child with extraordinary hand-eye coordination remain invisible because there is no shooting or archery facility nearby?

Talent does not know where we have built our infrastructure.

A child’s PIN code should not decide whether an ability is ever discovered. That is the truly exciting possibility before us: to democratise the discovery of talent. Having travelled the journey to an Olympic podium, I know that the medal is the smallest visible part of an athlete’s story. Before Athens came years of training, repetition, technical correction, competitions that went right and many that did not, coaches, family, discipline and opportunity. The medal came last. Long before excellence can be developed, potential has to be noticed.

India today has the opportunity to notice it earlier, wider and more scientifically than ever before. Not every child we assess will become an athlete. Nor should that be the expectation. But every child can become more aware of fitness.

Among millions of fitter children, thousands of exceptional physical abilities can be discovered. Among those thousands, the right children can be connected with the right sports and the right coaches. A larger talent pool creates stronger competition; stronger competition raises standards; and higher standards ultimately create champions. That is how India’s vast population becomes a demographic dividend for sport. The ambition, therefore, is beautifully simple: Fitness for every child. A pathway for every talent.

And somewhere in that enormous journey from fitness to excellence is a child who may stand on an Olympic podium in 2036. We don’t know the name yet. Perhaps even the child doesn’t know. But the country will.

(The author is an Olympic medallist, Athens 2004, former Union Minister for Youth Affairs & Sports, and Cabinet minister, Government of Rajasthan. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: 'Assalamualaikum' is Part of Indian Cultural Lexicon, Don’t Limit it to Religion
editorials.passage: Last year, in October, when Gwalior city SP Hina Khan raised the “Jai Shree Ram” slogan to combat an unruly crowd that was weaponising the slogan against her—in an effort to reduce her identity to barely her religion—it became a moment of reckoning. Khan had to raise the slogan to “diffuse” the situation, to deny the crowd the privilege of taking advantage of her identity. A year later, another SP, now in West Bengal, is trapped in a similar discursive trap: the burden of identity.  On 13 September, West Bengal Indian Police Service (IPS) officer Bushra Bano shared a video on how Aligarh Muslim University’s Coaching Centre helped her in the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) journey. The talk was nothing more than a motivation for UPSC aspirants. However, what was supposed to be a gesture of inspiration fractured when, a few days later,  the then-additional SP of Kharagpur was abruptly transferred to deputy commandant of the WB police. A simple talk became a matter of controversy when the Hindu Legal Fund, in their X account, said that they are filing a complaint against the officer.The reason? Bano began her speech with "Assalamualaikum", used "Insha'Allah", and ended with "Jazakallah”. It was said that a serving officer should “maintain neutrality” and only utilise “national expressions” in the public domain. Notably, the same tweet denounced her for not using “Vande Mataram” or “Jai Hind”. Khan Sir and the 'Good Muslim' TestIndeed, according to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules of 1968, Rule 3(1A)(ii), all serving members should maintain political neutrality. But when does using a socio-cultural vocabulary become a political manoeuvre? One might examine Bano’s alleged “misconduct” against the established AIS conduct rules. Under rule 6, officers do not require previous government sanctions to participate in public media, provided that they observe the provisions of the rules and they do not misrepresent personal views as those of the government. Bano’s video violates neither, as she merely presents her personal UPSC journey to motivate, with no references to anything that attacks the values of the government, or gives preferential treatment to any political or social ideology.Contrast this with the 2018 case of the former Director General (Home Guards) of UP, Surya Kumar Shukla, who was filmed taking a public pledge in a 2018 video for the early construction of Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. Despite pushback from the IPS association for violating “neutrality, fairness and uprightness”, Shukla faced minimal repercussions, aside from a procedural explanation to the government, which he brushed aside with abstract claims of maintaining communal harmony. He even had the backing of the UP State Principal Secretary (Home), who stated there was no need to seek further clarification from Shukla.What makes Shukla immune to action, even after visibly violating the code of conduct, whereas Bano is subjected to a transfer?Notably, days earlier, West Bengal witnessed an extensive Gerua Samman Yatra march, with crowds waving saffron flags as they chanted “Jai Shri Ram” and “Santaner Joy Hok”. Leading the march was none other than the newly elected Chief Minister of West Bengal, Suvendu Adhikari, who issued a warning that he would not tolerate “anyone uttering words or derogatory comments about [saffron]”. Reaching Jadavpur University, he stated that he knows “how to cleanse the campus of them”, referring to recent protests in favour of Palestine.'Is Bengal CM Scared of JU?': Suvendu Adhikari's Angry Speech Sparks QuestionsThis is, however, not an isolated event. In 2023, Prime Minister Narendra Modi installed a historic Tamil ‘Sengol’ in the Lok Sabha building. The PM sought the blessings of the Tamil high priests as they handed over the Sengol. After invoking the Gods through Ganpati Homam, he installed the Sengol amidst Vedic chants and nadaswaram. In 2024, the PM inaugurated the Ayodhya Temple, stating that “Our Lord Ram will be in a grand temple”. From declaring a holiday to marking this as a “new era”, the tone for the country’s future was set.In these moments, one couldn’t help but remember India’s first PM Jawaharlal Nehru’s displeasure at then-president Rajendra Prasad, who attended the inauguration of Somnath Temple. To Nehru, it was not “merely visiting a temple”, but rather upsetting the nation’s secularism by polarising communities and showing preferential treatment, especially as the Partition memory was still fresh. The evolution in the dominant culture of the state makes us ask a critical question: What are the “neutral” and “impartial” values? Do we need to measure it against an eternal “other”?Assaulted, Not Silenced: Muslim Women Journalists Who Refused to Be IntimidatedLastly, Assalamualeikum or Insha’Allah don’t represent Bano’s religious vocabulary, they are part of her cultural expressions. When many Indians casually say “Oh my God”, every time they are not essentially invoking any paradigmatic Christian connotation. Yet, the moment Allah or traditional Arabic greetings appear, they invoke suspicion.Why does every utterance of Insha'Allah have to carry exaggerated religious baggage, when for millions across the subcontinent, it is merely a reflex in situations for expressing hope or future intent? Finding religious connotation in every invocation of Allah, instead of considering it as a constitutive component of a composite linguistic framework, portrays an anachronistic worldview that has neither any idea about India’s history nor about its embedded multiculturality.(Halah Fathima is a writer and currently studies at Symbiosis School for Liberal Arts, Symbiosis International University. This is an opinion piece and the views expressed are the author's own. The Quint does not endorse or is responsible for them.
